items.mnemonic_text: 'What, ah, she?' — no, watashi means I.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a tanuki knocks over the shiny new security mirror by the till and freezes, nose to nose with itself. It taps the glass, tilts its head, and decides, flatly, that the animal staring back must be the most important customer in the store: itself. From then on it restocks the onigiri shelf for nobody else, certain of exactly who it means when it talks about I.

That fused, shoulder-to-shoulder answer is the meaning you want: we.

She grabs every item — onigiri, drinks, gum — and interrogates the shopper: what kind of rice is inside, what kind of flavor, what kind of wrapper. The beeping till never moves on until she gets an answer to her only question: what kind of.
items.reading_mnemonic: どんな is written exactly as it sounds — kana only, nothing to dig for — just read <reading>どんな</reading> straight through as it's written.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the enormous bell rings itself in the dead of night. The cats scatter, the mossy steps creak, and no one is standing anywhere near the rope. Grandma Kane storms out onto the steps demanding an answer to the only question that matters: who.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every night the bell rings and nobody's there, so Grandma Kane leans out over the mossy steps and bellows into the dark: who <reading>dares</reading> touch my bell? The cats scatter at the challenge in her voice, and that same dare is exactly the sound of <reading>だれ</reading> — the question of who it could possibly be.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, past the lone vending machine, a hiker meets a stranger wrapped head to toe against the wind. Too winded to be casual, they bow deeply and ask with careful formality: might I ask, to whom do I have the honor of speaking? The mountain answers only with silence, and the polite question just hangs there: who, respectfully asked.
items.reading_mnemonic: どなた is written exactly as it sounds, kana only — read straight through as <reading>どなた</reading>, no hidden reading to derive.
items.description: This is the polite version of the plain word for who, used when asking after a stranger, a guest, or anyone you would address formally, the way English shifts from a blunt who's that to who, may I ask. Save the plain form for friends and family instead.

example_sentences.furigana: どなたと一[いっ]緒[しょ]に行[い]きますか。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A frazzled nanny in the echoing hallways of Sei's school is handed things by a toddler all morning: a wet sock, half a stapler, a beetle that is still alive. She has stopped guessing what any of it is. She just holds each object out at arm's length and asks the one flat question that covers all of it — what.
items.reading_mnemonic: The same <reading>nanny</reading> takes a night shift at Koichi's konbini, and every time the beeping till coughs up an item she does not recognise she holds it over the onigiri shelf and says <reading>なに</reading> at the ceiling. By closing she has said it forty times and solved nothing.
items.description: On its own — as a bare question, or with most particles — the word takes this reading. When a counter, the plain copula, or a word beginning with a t, d, or n sound follows, it switches to the shorter reading you learn separately.

items.mnemonic_text: nani shortened to nan before counters.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Cats keep arriving on the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine, and you gave up asking what a cat is hours ago. Every question you have left comes with a number stuck to it: how many cats, what floor they have reached, what time they stop. This is the shape the question takes when a counter follows — what, before counters.
items.reading_mnemonic: A tiny <reading>nun</reading> has claimed the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail and runs it like a ticket window. She will not press a button until you say <reading>なん</reading> and then the counter for what you want, and she makes you start again if you mumble the number.
items.description: This is the same word as the standalone question, wearing the shape it takes when a counter, the plain copula, or a word beginning with a t, d, or n sound follows it. You almost never meet it alone; it arrives glued to whatever is being counted.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A heron standing in the shallows at the riverbank wears a wristwatch and answers questions for free. You ask about the water going down: it's two. You ask about the ferry: it's two. You ask about getting your own watch back off its leg: it's two. Ask a heron anything and it hands you a time, so the question you are really asking is when.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it is said, so <reading>いつ</reading> is both the spelling and the reading — nothing to decode.
items.description: English lets you say when for both the question and the joining word, as in the sentence about what happens when it rains. This word only does the question. The joining sense uses different grammar entirely.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a fisherman reels in his line for the ninth time and finds nothing but a waterlogged boot, same as the last eight. He doesn't swear, doesn't sigh — he just plants his feet in the mud, glares at the current, and asks the only question left standing: why.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>なぜ</reading>.
items.description: なぜ reads as blunter and more formal than a casual why — common in writing, official questions, and pointed interrogation. Dropped into an ordinary chat with a friend, on its own it can land as accusatory rather than merely curious.

example_sentences.japanese: なぜ今日忙しいですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼はなぜ帰りませんか。

example_sentences.english: Why do you read that book?
example_sentences.furigana: なぜその本[ほん]を読[よ]みますか。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till beeps and charges double for the same onigiri, for the third night running. Koichi stares at the receipt under the fluorescent lights, not with a customer's cool complaint but a genuine, immediate splutter — why, how come, what is going on here.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: <reading>どうして</reading>.
items.description: どうして carries more feeling than a neutral question — it often doubles as an exclamation of surprise or frustration, how did this even happen, rather than a calm request for a reason, and it's the version heard far more in casual conversation than in writing.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, one impossible vending machine hums between the trees, accepting a coin no one on the trail carries. A hiker who just spent an hour climbing pokes button after button, turns to a stranger nearby, and asks the only sensible question left: how does this thing even work.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane catches a cat dragging a rice offering off the shrine's mossy steps. Instead of shouting, she bows a fraction and asks, syrupy with formality, how the day has been treating it. The cat freezes mid-theft, offering still in its mouth, trapped by the world's politest how. Courtesy, not curiosity, is the whole word.

Koichi starts counting, and halfway through, the kid swivels and asks the identical question about his age. The tower wobbles, forgotten, as Koichi answers both with the same flat number — how many and how old are one demand wearing two coats to this kid.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker drags himself up the mountain trail to the vending machine improbably waiting at the top, expecting water. The display keeps climbing past every price he's paid for a drink, digit by digit, as he jabs the button asking how much this could possibly cost. It never stops long enough to answer — the only punchline the machine needs.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is written in kana exactly as it sounds: 「<reading>いくら</reading>」.
items.description: いくら written this way is also the everyday word for salmon roe, the bright orange fish eggs served over rice — a completely different word that happens to share the same sound and spelling. Context sorts them out fast: paired with a price or a question, it means how much; sitting on a plate, it means the food.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the team spends the entire match slipping on the wet grass, missing every shot, while the goalkeeper falls asleep against the post. The final whistle blows, the scoreboard locks in one flat, humiliating number, and the whole bench stares at it in silence. That number is zero.

items.description: ゼロ is the everyday spoken form, heard in scores, phone numbers, and casual temperature talk; formal or written contexts often reach for a different, more formal word instead.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, a ranger posts an official notice board each morning with the exact temperature. One frost-bitten dawn, the mercury refuses to rise past the middle line at all, and the ranger stamps the report with one stiff, formal number before trudging back down. That number is zero.

items.description: 零 is the formal, written register for zero — the word you'd see on an official temperature report or hear in a stiff announcement, not the one you'd use casually reading out a phone number or a game score.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Judging her own talent show yet again, the smug goat holds up a single hoof and announces the score before anyone can ask: <kanji>one</kanji> out of one. There was only ever one entrant, one stage, one strip of dirt to stand on, so the number was settled before the show even began. She says it like a verdict, not a count: one.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A teacher taps a chalk pointer against three stacked lines on the board, one, two, three, and by the third tap the class already knows what word is coming before she says it. There is no trick to uncover here: <kanji>three</kanji> lines stacked in a character just spells the word three, plainly, the way it has all along.

That flattened stare is the number stamped on this word: <kanji>four</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the gym teacher drags out the fourth roll call of the morning, already worn thin. He tips his head back for one long, stagey <reading>yawn</reading> before barking the count down the echoing hallway: a flat <reading>よん</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: The alternate, ominous reading of four: shi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the same sealed box waits among the mossy steps, its trapped mouth still murmuring numbers into the corner. A cat swats it off the step and the lid cracks — the mouth peeks out just far enough to hiss a hushed <kanji>four</kanji> before a monk claps the lid shut, refusing to let it say the number again.
items.reading_mnemonic: That hushed <reading>し</reading> is the same reading 四 already taught you — the clipped <reading>shh</reading> the monk uses to cut the mouth off mid-count.
items.description: This reading of 四 sounds identical to a much darker word, so hospitals, hotels, and gift-givers avoid it — floor numbers, room numbers, and counted items switch to the other reading, よん, instead. Learn to recognize both, but default to よん when you're the one speaking.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, that same hooked hand reaches out from beside the vending machine, snagging snacks lined along the ledge. It's already got four stacked in your arms when the crooked hook swipes once more and lands a fifth off the top shelf. One hook, five snacks: that's the word for <kanji>five</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: That practiced swipe already speaks the <reading>ご</reading> reading you learned for 五 — the clipped <reading>go</reading> you mutter to yourself right before you reach.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, eight cats are sprawled across the mossy steps at dawn. She sets the heavy iron offering lid down with a clang right on the top step, and two cats bolt at the sound, tails high. What's left staring up at the enormous bell is <kanji>six</kanji> cats, thoroughly unimpressed by the racket. The lid on top of eight, as always, leaves <kanji>six</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 六's reading here is just the number's own reading you already learned: <reading>ろく</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: By the door of Koichi's konbini, the coat hook is really just one bent nail sticking out of the wall. You can feel it waiting just behind the horizon, ready to flood in the moment this window opens again. The day still queued up behind that glass is tomorrow.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The trailing runner is so far <kanji>behind</kanji> the pack he misses today's finish line entirely. He staggers past the sun's <kanji>day</kanji> window just as it flips shut — then flips shut again before he arrives. Two whole days close inside that window before he shows up, so nobody calls it tomorrow. It's the day after tomorrow.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's vending machine, a hiker drops a salty tray of dried squid clean over the edge. It bounces ledge to ledge so long that two sunrises pass before it clatters to a stop below, and by then everyone agrees the <reading>a salty tray</reading> landed on <reading>あさって</reading> — the day after tomorrow.

Two windows back is where she finds it: the day before yesterday.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は来月学校に行きます。
example_sentences.english: He's going to school next month.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は来[らい]月[げつ]学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Those two legs, already <kanji>ahead</kanji> of everyone, are long gone before you've even reached the door. By the time you catch up, the sliver of <kanji>month</kanji> they left under has faded to nothing and grown back new. Whatever they did, they did it under last month's crescent.
items.reading_mnemonic: 先 already gives you せん and 月 already gives you げつ — lay them end to end into <reading>せんげつ</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 先月映画を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I watched a movie last month.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]月[げつ]映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 先月は忙しかったです。
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]月[げつ]は忙[いそが]しかったです。

example_sentences.japanese: 先月友達と公園に行きました。
example_sentences.english: I went to the park with a friend last month.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]月[げつ]友[とも]達[だち]と公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You invite the scarecrow to take cover under the roof right <kanji>now</kanji>. It's used to standing out in the weather for a full <kanji>year</kanji> at a time, but you decide it deserves to stay inside for this year.
items.reading_mnemonic: You find the scarecrow shivering in the snow, so you give her a thick winter <reading>coat. She</reading> puts it on with her stiff straw arms, grateful that <reading>ことし</reading> she won't freeze.

example_sentences.japanese: 今年は忙しいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 今年[ことし]は忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 今年、彼女に会います。
example_sentences.furigana: 今年[ことし]、彼[かの]女[じょ]に会[あ]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 今年は海に行きました。
example_sentences.english: I went to the ocean this year.
example_sentences.furigana: 今年[ことし]は海[うみ]に行[い]きました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The tree at the crossroads waves its branches at the scarecrow, telling it to <kanji>come</kanji> rest in the shade. The scarecrow yells back that it has to stand in the field for the rest of the <kanji>year</kanji>, but promises to finally take a break next year.
items.reading_mnemonic: The reading is exactly what you learned for the kanji: 来 (らい) plus 年 (ねん) makes <reading>らいねん</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 来年海に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I'm going to the sea next year.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]年[ねん]海[うみ]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 来年は忙しいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]年[ねん]は忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 来年友達と映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I'll watch a movie with a friend next year.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]年[ねん]友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You walk up to the scarecrow that has been silently watching the field for a whole <kanji>year</kanji>. Its straw arms are sagging and birds have built nests in its hat, clearly showing that it has been stuck out here since last year.
items.reading_mnemonic: You are directing a play starring the scarecrow, but it keeps missing its <reading>cue. Nena</reading>, your stage manager, sighs and reminds you that it was much better at acting <reading>きょねん</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 去年、友達と海に行きました。
example_sentences.english: Last year I went to the sea with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 去[きょ]年[ねん]、友[とも]達[だち]と海[うみ]に行[い]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は去年この本を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought this book last year.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は去[きょ]年[ねん]この本[ほん]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 去年は忙しかったです。
example_sentences.furigana: 去[きょ]年[ねん]は忙[いそが]しかったです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the <kanji>time</kanji>-sun still crawls its slow arc overhead. A dazed tourist wanders in, squinting up, unable to read a single hour off it, and grabs a passing cat to blurt the same question over and over: <kanji>what</kanji> <kanji>time</kanji> is it? Her whole visit is just that one question: what time.
items.reading_mnemonic: 何 reads なん here and 時 keeps じ, combining straight into <reading>なんじ</reading> — exactly what you would expect when asking the time.

example_sentences.japanese: 今何時ですか。
example_sentences.furigana: 今[いま]何[なん]時[じ]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 何時に起きますか。
example_sentences.english: What time do you get up?
example_sentences.furigana: 何[なに]時[じ]に起[お]きますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 映画は何時ですか。
example_sentences.furigana: 映[えい]画[が]は何[なん]時[じ]ですか。

items.mnemonic_text: The interval of the sun: jikan.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You are tracking the <kanji>time</kanji> by watching the sun climb the sky. But when it hits the <kanji>interval</kanji> of the open gate, the sun gets completely wedged in the gap. It stops moving, which means all the time / hours in the world have frozen.
items.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made of kanji you already learned, the reading is just <reading>じかん</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今は時間がありません。
example_sentences.english: I don't have time right now.
example_sentences.furigana: 今[いま]は時[じ]間[かん]がありません。

example_sentences.japanese: 二時間待ちました。
example_sentences.furigana: 二[に]時[じ]間[かん]待[ま]ちました。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達と遊ぶ時間があります。
example_sentences.english: I have time to hang out with friends.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]と遊[あそ]ぶ時[じ]間[かん]があります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the shrine's mossy steps the shadow post and its ruler announce the <kanji>hour</kanji>, and the woodcutter beside it handles everything smaller: one log, one <kanji>minute</kanji>, two halves leaning apart with a cat asleep on each. The cats can tell you exactly what time of day it is by counting the woodpile.
items.reading_mnemonic: 時 keeps the じ you already know and 分 its ぶん, so this one reads straight through as <reading>じぶん</reading>.
items.description: 時分 is dated and bookish — modern speech uses plain time expressions instead. The same reading also belongs to a far commoner word meaning oneself, so context, not sound, tells you which is meant.

example_sentences.japanese: 今時分はもう夜です。
example_sentences.english: It's already night around this time of day.
example_sentences.furigana: 今[いま]時[じ]分[ぶん]はもう夜[よる]です。

example_sentences.japanese: この時分は寒いです。
example_sentences.english: It's cold at this time of day.
example_sentences.furigana: この時[じ]分[ぶん]は寒[さむ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 昼の時分にご飯を食べます。
example_sentences.furigana: 昼[ひる]の時[じ]分[ぶん]にご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You are buying an onigiri at the fluorescent-bright convenience store. The cashier hits a button on the beeping till and announces you have exactly one second to hand over your cash. You panic and throw your wallet at the counter, terrified of how fast a single second passes.
items.reading_mnemonic: The wallet sails through the air, but a person standing right <reading>by you</reading> (<reading>びょう</reading>) snatches it. They pocket your money and walk out the door, leaving you to spend your last second in total disbelief.

example_sentences.japanese: 十秒待ちます。
example_sentences.furigana: 十[じゅう]秒[びょう]待[ま]ちます。

example_sentences.japanese: 三秒見てください。
example_sentences.furigana: 三[さん]秒[びょう]見[み]てください。

example_sentences.japanese: 今、三十秒です。
example_sentences.furigana: 今[いま]、三[さん]十[じゅう]秒[びょう]です。

items.mnemonic_text: A part of the hour: fun.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The sword that redeemed itself on that first log has found steady work at the school: the woodcutter stands at the edge of the sports field and splits one every time the runners set off. Log down, two halves leaning apart, whistle. Nobody there owns a stopwatch, so a single split log is exactly one <kanji>minute</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 分 uses the very reading you learned with the kanji itself, so on its own it is just <reading>ふん</reading>.
items.description: 分 is the counter for minutes and almost never stands alone; it follows a number, and after some of them (one, three, four, six, eight, ten) its sound shifts from an f-sound to a p-sound.

example_sentences.japanese: 五分待ちます。
example_sentences.furigana: 五[ご]分[ふん]待[ま]ちます。

example_sentences.japanese: 十分で帰ります。
example_sentences.english: I'll head home in ten minutes.
example_sentences.furigana: 十[じゅう]分[ふん]で帰[かえ]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 三分だけ本を読みます。
example_sentences.english: I'll read a book for just three minutes.
example_sentences.furigana: 三[さん]分[ふん]だけ本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You stare at the clock as the minute hand hits the bottom, turning the face into a giant exclamation point split right down the middle. That exact moment when the hour is chopped in <kanji>half</kanji> means it is half (past).
items.reading_mnemonic: Since you already know the reading for this kanji, you know the reading for this word is <reading>はん</reading>.
items.description: You will see this attached directly to hour counters to say half past the hour.

example_sentences.japanese: 今は九時半です。
example_sentences.furigana: 今[いま]は九[きゅう]時[じ]半[はん]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 七時半に起きます。
example_sentences.furigana: 七[なな]時[じ]半[はん]に起[お]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達と二時半に会います。
example_sentences.english: I'm meeting a friend at two-thirty.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]と二[に]時[じ]半[はん]に会[あ]います。

items.mnemonic_text: The end of the week: shuumatsu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You trace the winding path for the <kanji>week</kanji> until you run out of calendar page completely and your finger slips off the paper. Dropping off the edge of that grid lands you right in the weekend.
items.reading_mnemonic: You spend your entire weekend at the riverbank scrubbing the mud out of your car's <reading>shoe mats</reading> (<reading>しゅうまつ</reading>). You wash them for two days straight, completely ruining your actual weekend.

example_sentences.japanese: 週末に公園で遊びます。
example_sentences.english: I hang out at the park on the weekend.
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]に公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: この週末は映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I'm watching a movie this weekend.
example_sentences.furigana: この週[しゅう]末[まつ]は映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 週末は友達とご飯を食べます。
example_sentences.english: On the weekend I eat with friends.
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]は友[とも]達[だち]とご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You peer through a window at the <kanji>sun</kanji>, only to realize it is just a painting inside a massive <kanji>weekday</kanji> calendar square. Before you can process the trick, a real <kanji>sun</kanji> rises behind it and sets the whole paper structure on fire to celebrate Sunday.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know the readings for the kanji in this word, so you just put them together to get <reading>にちようび</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 日曜日に公園で遊びます。
example_sentences.english: I play at the park on Sunday.
example_sentences.furigana: 日[にち]曜[よう]日[ひ]に公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 日曜日の夜に映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I watch a movie on Sunday night.
example_sentences.furigana: 日[にち]曜[よう]日[ひ]の夜[よる]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 日曜日は友達と会います。
example_sentences.english: I meet my friends on Sunday.
example_sentences.furigana: 日[にち]曜[よう]日[ひ]は友[とも]達[だち]と会[あ]います。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The squawking birds on your <kanji>weekday</kanji> calendar square are completely asleep under a thin crescent <kanji>moon</kanji>. They stubbornly refuse to wake up and look at the window showing the morning <kanji>sun</kanji>, because everyone is too exhausted on Monday.
items.reading_mnemonic: Since you learned the readings for these kanji already, combining them gives you <reading>げつようび</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 月曜日に学校に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to school on Monday.
example_sentences.furigana: 月[げつ]曜[よう]日[ひ]に学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 来週の月曜日は忙しいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]週[しゅう]の月[げつ]曜[よう]日[ひ]は忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 月曜日の朝、コーヒーを飲みます。
example_sentences.english: I drink coffee on Monday morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 月[げつ]曜[よう]日[ひ]の朝[あさ]、コーヒーを飲[の]みます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You flip your calendar to check the <kanji>weekday</kanji>, but the square for today's <kanji>day</kanji> is completely charred. Looking closely, a tiny sparking figure made of <kanji>fire</kanji> is running around inside the window frame, burning up the paper. You sigh. The calendar always bursts into flames on Tuesday.
items.reading_mnemonic: Since you already know the reading for each kanji, you can simply put them together to form <reading>かようび</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 火曜日に映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I'll watch a movie on Tuesday.
example_sentences.furigana: 火[か]曜[よう]日[ひ]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日は火曜日です。
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]は火[か]曜[よう]日[ひ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 来週の火曜日に友達と会います。
example_sentences.english: I'll meet a friend next Tuesday.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]週[しゅう]の火[か]曜[よう]日[ひ]に友[とも]達[だち]と会[あ]います。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>weekday</kanji>, you stand by the riverbank to watch the <kanji>sun</kanji> come up, but today a massive geyser of freezing <kanji>water</kanji> blasts out of the river and knocks you flat into the mud. You scrape yourself off, remembering that this mid-week flood always happens on Wednesday.
items.reading_mnemonic: There are no new sounds to learn here, just combine the kanji readings you already know into <reading>すいようび</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 水曜日は忙しいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 水[すい]曜[よう]日[ひ]は忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 水曜日に友達と遊びます。
example_sentences.english: I hang out with friends on Wednesday.
example_sentences.furigana: 水[すい]曜[よう]日[ひ]に友[とも]達[だち]と遊[あそ]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 水曜日の午後、家に帰ります。
example_sentences.english: I go home on Wednesday afternoon.
example_sentences.furigana: 水[すい]曜[よう]日[ひ]の午[ご]後[ご]、家[いえ]に帰[かえ]ります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You arrive at Sei's school for a normal <kanji>weekday</kanji> of classes, but looking out the window, a massive <kanji>tree</kanji> has smashed right through the sports field to block out the <kanji>sun</kanji>. The principal announces over the intercom that classes are cancelled, which is typical for Thursday.
items.reading_mnemonic: You can sound this word out by stringing together the readings you learned for its component kanji to get <reading>もくようび</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 木曜日に学校に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to school on Thursday.
example_sentences.furigana: 木[もく]曜[よう]日[ひ]に学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 木曜日は忙しいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 木[もく]曜[よう]日[ひ]は忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 来週の木曜日に会います。
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]週[しゅう]の木[もく]曜[よう]日[ひ]に会[あ]います。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You go into Koichi's konbini to buy a single onigiri to start your <kanji>day</kanji>. When the till beeps, Koichi doesn't ask for regular yen; he demands a literal pile of <kanji>gold</kanji>. You complain that this is the only <kanji>weekday</kanji> he does this, and hand over your treasure because it is Friday.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is completely regular, so just read the kanji exactly as you learned them to get <reading>きんようび</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は金曜日です。
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は金[きん]曜[よう]日[ひ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 金曜日に友達と会います。
example_sentences.english: I'm meeting a friend on Friday.
example_sentences.furigana: 金[きん]曜[よう]日[ひ]に友[とも]達[だち]と会[あ]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 来週の金曜日、映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: Next Friday, I'll watch a movie.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]週[しゅう]の金[きん]曜[よう]日[ひ]、映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the calendar, Saturday's square holds a wooden cross planted into the page, dirt piling around its base — <kanji>earth</kanji> dug into the paper. Beside it crowds a tangle of feathers marking the square as a <kanji>weekday</kanji>, while a windowed frame shows the sun climbing to start the <kanji>day</kanji>: earth, weekday, and day stacked on one square make Saturday.
items.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just the pieces you already know lined up in order: 土（ど）＋曜（よう）＋日（び）＝<reading>どようび</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 土曜日に公園で遊びます。
example_sentences.english: I play at the park on Saturday.
example_sentences.furigana: 土[ど]曜[よう]日[ひ]に公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 土曜日は家で本を読みます。
example_sentences.english: On Saturday I read a book at home.
example_sentences.furigana: 土[ど]曜[よう]日[ひ]は家[いえ]で本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 来週の土曜日に会いましょう。
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]週[しゅう]の土[ど]曜[よう]日[ひ]に会[あ]いましょう。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The smug goat's one-contestant talent show — one stage, one prize, one judge, all her — only ever opens the instant the sun first climbs through the windowed frame of a brand new <kanji>day</kanji>. She refuses to be anything but <kanji>one</kanji>, so she insists on staging it the very moment each month's sun rises for the first time, never later. That stubborn need to go first, first day, every single month: the 1st.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane opens the shrine on the very first morning of the month and finds her legs unbearably <reading>too itchy</reading> — poison ivy from clearing the mossy steps. She scratches through the whole ceremony, grumbling that the reading for this day, <reading>ついたち</reading>, always shows up with an itch she can't shake.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日は一日です。
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]は一日[ついたち]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 一日に友達と会います。
example_sentences.english: I'll meet a friend on the 1st.
example_sentences.furigana: 一[いち]日[にち]に友[とも]達[だち]と会[あ]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 今月の一日は忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: The 1st of this month is busy.
example_sentences.furigana: 今[こん]月[げつ]の一日[ついたち]は忙[いそが]しいです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The raccoon's broth has already gone cold once, but true to form, a second raccoon slips in and snaps its own chopstick to match the <kanji>two</kanji> lines exactly — and it only ever happens after the sun has climbed back through the window to open a fresh <kanji>day</kanji>. By the time the matching ritual is finished, that first day is gone and a second one has quietly started: two days, four paws, still nobody eating.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini clerk trips over the same forgotten mop bucket two mornings running and lands flat on his back, socks soaked both times, groaning that his feet have gone <reading>footsore</reading>. Everyone at the register agrees this is just how <reading>ふつか</reading> goes — the second day is always the one that actually gets you.

example_sentences.japanese: 二日学校に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I'm going to school on the 2nd.
example_sentences.furigana: 二日[ふつか]学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達が二日来ます。
example_sentences.english: A friend is coming for two days.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]が二日[ふつか]来[き]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日は二日です。
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]は二日[ふつか]です。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Stack the <kanji>three</kanji> flat lines on top of each other and each one turns out to be its own tiny windowed frame with a sun climbing up through it — a triple-decker calendar. One <kanji>day</kanji> passes on the bottom line, then the middle one lights up, then the top, and the sun never bothers waiting around for a fourth: three days, no more, no less.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei collapses after the third whistle blast on the sports field, and the nurse says she's gone <reading>meeker</reading> by the hour — flu, straight home for <reading>みっか</reading>, three full days in bed before anyone lets her back on the field.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は三日です。
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は三[みっ]日[か]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 三日待ちます。
example_sentences.furigana: 三[みっ]日[か]待[ま]ちます。

example_sentences.japanese: 三日、友達と遊びました。
example_sentences.english: I played with a friend for three days.
example_sentences.furigana: 三[みっ]日[か]、友[とも]達[だち]と遊[あそ]びました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Trapped inside the enclosure, the mouth keeps counting under its breath, and on the try that decides everything it finally lands on <kanji>four</kanji>. The instant it shouts the number, the window's bar snaps back and the <kanji>sun</kanji> pours through into a brand new <kanji>day</kanji>. Four counted breaths, one sunrise — that's the 4th, four days gone.
items.reading_mnemonic: 四's reading よっ and 日's reading か combine straight into <reading>よっか</reading>, exactly the regular reading you'd expect for four days.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The bent nail hook holds seven coats until one more lands and it creaks under the weight, confirming <kanji>seven</kanji>. items.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>day</kanji> the sun climbs through its window and lights the same crack in the riverbank ice — a crack shaped exactly like the splitting legs of <kanji>eight</kanji>. Each sunrise splits it wider: one, two, three, all the way to the eighth. By the eighth sunrise the ice has split clean into two drifting halves, eight days of widening, and it's officially the eighth.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every <kanji>day</kanji> the sun climbs through its window and finds you at the shrine steps, raising both hands a little higher than yesterday, palms open like the <kanji>ten</kanji>-shaped cross you make once all your fingers are up. Nine sunrises of half-raised hands pass before the tenth, when both hands finally form that perfect cross overhead — ten days of raising, and it's the tenth.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word takes 十's reading とお and 日's reading か and fuses them together, giving 「<reading>とおか</reading>」: the 10th, ten days.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The two raccoons are still hunched over their cold noodle broth, each guarding its snapped chopstick — the same two you met before. Every <kanji>day</kanji> new sun through the window finds them arranging the four chopstick halves into one perfect cross, the shape of <kanji>ten</kanji>, then doubling that cross because there are <kanji>two</kanji> raccoons at the table. After twenty of these sunrises nobody has eaten a single noodle: the twentieth day.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer grabs coffee straight off the warmer and spills it across the hood of his parked <reading>hot car</reading> right by the beeping till. Twenty days running he does this at checkout, and the staff now just call it <reading>はつか</reading> — the 20th, twenty days of the same scalded hood.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Zookeeper Zoe stopped filing her animals by species years ago. Now every enclosure is sorted by family: otters piled into one <kanji>house</kanji>, meerkats packed into one den, and the daily headcount sheet has only one column, because at her zoo the only unit that ever matters is the whole family showing up together.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini you're bragging to the clerk about how your father rewired the flickering sign himself. But every time the word for father leaves your mouth it comes out clipped and small, a fast double note like a chick cheeping under the counter, because that's the plain, low-key way you refer to your own father, never anyone else's.
items.reading_mnemonic: A chick has gotten loose behind Koichi's register and won't stop cheeping two identical notes at the customers. The sound lands exactly like <reading>ちち</reading>, the same clipped double <reading>chee-chee</reading> twice in a row, and it's the one word stuck to that particular chirp from now on.
items.description: 父 (chichi) is the plain, humble word for your own father, used only when talking about him to people outside the family — never for someone else's father, and not usually what you'd call him to his face. お父さん (otousan) is the polite counterpart: what you call your own dad directly, or how you refer to someone else's father.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, red-faced and sweating under the noon sun, a father hauls a stalled cart the last hundred meters by rope while his kid cheers from beside the lone vending machine. That's the picture pinned to father, polite: the dad you'd point out respectfully to a stranger, not the tired grumble you'd use at home.
items.reading_mnemonic: As he heaves the cart past the vending machine, the kid shouts the word for him, and it lands in your ear as <reading>oh, tow, sun</reading> — dad towing, sun blazing overhead — the same beats as <reading>おとうさん</reading>. That's the polite word for pointing him out to a stranger on the trail, not the plain one for talking about your own.
items.description: お父さん (otousan) is the polite, respectful word for father — what you call your own dad directly, or how you refer to someone else's father in conversation. It contrasts with the plain 父 (chichi), which you use only when talking about your own father to people outside the family.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, among the mossy steps and the cats sprawled everywhere, your mother doubles over laughing at some joke only she finds funny, the sound bouncing flat off the one enormous bell. That plain, unpolished laugh is exactly the humble word you use for your own mother, never for anyone else's.

items.description: 母 (haha) is the plain, humble word for your own mother, used when speaking about her to people outside the family — never for someone else's mother, and not typically what you call her to her face. It contrasts with お母さん (okaasan), the polite form used to address your own mother directly or refer to someone else's.

Then his mother crests the rise behind him, unbothered, carrying his backpack, her water bottle, and a spare pair of socks, somehow not out of breath. That endless, unglamorous readiness is what mother (polite) means.

The kids in the back seat brace and yell <reading>oh, car, san</reading> — which is exactly how <reading>おかあさん</reading> sounds, screamed by children who have done this drive with her before.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the last good onigiri is one shelf away. Your older brother doesn't ask — he plants a hand on your shoulder, uses you as a step stool, and takes it while you're still off balance. That casual, lifelong right to shove you aside without apologizing is what (my) older brother names.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, he shoves past you and you catch the shelf edge with your knee. <reading>Ah, knee</reading>, you groan, doubled over by the onigiri — which is exactly how <reading>あに</reading> sounds, and exactly who just walked off without noticing.

Nobody there is related to him, but everyone calls him older brother (polite) anyway, because that is simply what the word is for.

She lines up the little ones, ties their shoelaces, and lets them win. That respectful, polite way you address someone's honored older sister is exactly this word.

items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the small brother stomps on the same customer's foot twice reaching for onigiri, and the customer yelps <reading>oh, toe, toe</reading> each time. The beeping till clerk sighs and says it again, plain: <reading>おとうと</reading>, always causing trouble.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the old bell-ringer finally hands the rope to someone new: a stooped man with a walking stick who has swept the mossy steps every morning for forty years. The cats accept him instantly. The children bow and call him grandfather, and from that day the enormous bell is his alone to ring.
items.reading_mnemonic: おじいさん is written exactly as it sounds, so there's no reading to decode — just the kana <reading>おじいさん</reading> read straight through.
items.description: おじいさん politely addresses or refers to any elderly man, related or not — closer to how English speakers might greet a stranger as "grandpa" than a strict family term.

example_sentences.japanese: おじいさんは本を読む。
example_sentences.furigana: おじいさんは本[ほん]を読[よ]む。

example_sentences.japanese: 私のおじいさんはお茶を飲む。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]のおじいさんはお茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]む。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、おじいさんの家に行く。
example_sentences.english: Tomorrow I'm going to grandfather's house.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、おじいさんの家[いえ]に行[い]く。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till goes quiet as an elderly woman — an <kanji>ancestor</kanji> in her own right, and someone's <kanji>mother</kanji> long before she became a grandmother — counts her coins one by one. Koichi leans over to the new hire and says simply: that's my grandmother, in for her onigiri. No polite title, no fuss — just family, plain and direct, the way you describe your own grandmother to someone else.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word takes 祖's reading そ and 母's reading ぼ and fuses them together, giving 「<reading>そぼ</reading>」: (my) grandmother.
items.description: 祖母 is how you refer to your own grandmother when speaking to someone outside the family — plain and humble, with no polite title attached. It isn't what you'd call her directly, or use for someone else's grandmother, both of which take an address term instead.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の祖母は本を読みます。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の祖[そ]母[ぼ]は本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 週末に祖母と公園へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: On the weekend I go to the park with my grandmother.

example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、祖[そ]母[ぼ]に会[あ]いました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank where the washing happens, an old woman scrubs scarves for the whole village and refuses anyone's help. Children stop to greet her properly before crossing, and she waves them on with damp hands. To everyone nearby, respectfully, she's simply grandmother — polite, warm, and impossible to argue with.
items.reading_mnemonic: おばあさん is written exactly as it sounds, so there's no reading to decode — just the kana <reading>おばあさん</reading> read straight through.
items.description: おばあさん politely addresses or refers to any elderly woman, related or not — closer to how English speakers might greet a stranger as "ma'am" than a strict family term.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, past the point where most people turn back, a man in hiking boots is refilling the lone vending machine himself — turns out it's your uncle, who apparently owns the machine and hikes up every week just to restock it. Nobody in the family questions this anymore. That's just what your uncle does.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, a hiker rounds the last switchback and yelps, oh, gee, at the stranger already there. It's not a stranger — it's your uncle, and that startled gasp is exactly <reading>おじ</reading>: <reading>oh, gee</reading>, uncle, fancy meeting you up here.
items.description: 叔父 marks a younger uncle — your parent's younger brother, or one married in — as distinct from the term for an older uncle, though both get shortened to the same casual address form in speech.

example_sentences.japanese: 叔父と公園で遊んだ。
example_sentences.english: I played with my uncle at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 叔父[おじ]と公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]んだ。

example_sentences.japanese: 週末、叔父の家に行く。
example_sentences.english: On the weekend, I go to my uncle's house.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, an aunt turns up every New Year wrapped in an absurd sheep-print scarf. The temple cats scatter, certain a sheep has invaded their mossy steps. Flustered, she throws up both hands and calls out across the courtyard — that startled, scarf-wrapped arrival is exactly who aunt means.
items.reading_mnemonic: As the cats bolt, she cries <reading>Oh, baa!</reading> — sheep noise, not sheep, just her own flustered yelp. That startled cry, <reading>おば</reading>, is the exact sound of an aunt arriving at Grandma Kane's shrine every single year, scarf and all.
items.description: The vowel here is short — don't stretch it into the longer sound used for the word for grandmother. They look and sound almost identical on the page but name different relatives, so lean on the mnemonic's short, startled yelp to keep the vowel length honest.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の叔母は毎朝コーヒーを飲みます。
example_sentences.english: My aunt drinks coffee every morning.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That swaddled <kanji>child</kanji>, arms still flung wide from its own story, wriggles loose right in Koichi's konbini and topples half the onigiri shelf reaching for it. The till beeps in protest as a clerk calls out for whoever's kid this troublemaker belongs to — arms flailing, wrapping gone, still unmistakably a child.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word takes 子's reading こ and adds 供's reading ども, giving 「<reading>こども</reading>」: child.

example_sentences.english: A child plays in the park.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same swaddled <kanji>child</kanji>, arms flung wide, has somehow hauled itself up the whole mountain trail and is now feeding coins into the vending machine at the summit like it owns the place. A hiker asks the panting father trailing behind whose kid that is. He beams, chest out — that's his son.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the summit, the father spots a moose eyeing his boy's snack and bellows <reading>Moose, Coe!</reading> — the name of the trail's resident moose, shouted fast and clipped. That exact bark, <reading>むすこ</reading>, is what every hiker on this mountain learns to recognize as a warning about his son.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the sports field at Sei's school, a girl in oversized cleats trips over the finish-line ribbon and drags the whole banner down with her. A woman in the stands leaps up, mortified and delighted at once, shouting across the entire field for her — this ribbon-tangled little disaster is her daughter.
items.reading_mnemonic: Still tangled in ribbon, she turns to the snack table and asks sweetly, <reading>Mousse, may?</reading> — polite as anything in the middle of a disaster. That well-mannered request, <reading>むすめ</reading>, is the reading you're listening for.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の娘は学校に行きます。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の娘[むすめ]は学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>person</kanji> striding forward suddenly stops and throws their arms out wide, legs spread as far as they'll go — the stance for showing off something <kanji>big</kanji>. Nobody teaches a kid to stand like that; you grow into needing the room. Standing tall enough to need the whole stance is what makes you an adult.
items.reading_mnemonic: Dai the giant baby stops wailing the second someone hands him <reading>a tuna</reading> — the calm is instant, like a switch. Jin ducks through the doorway just in time to see it: <reading>おとな</reading>, grown up right in front of him.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture two toddlers wedged together at Koichi's konbini, gripping the same onigiri, each wailing that the other one started it. One throws back a gaping yawn like the <kanji>older brother</kanji> who owns the place, while the other trails a loop of cord like the <kanji>younger brother</kanji> showing off a stolen bow. Neither releases, and the clerk just watches the same tantrum play out twice — that tangled squabble is what siblings means.

items.mnemonic_text: The master of the house: goshujin.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>person</kanji> who strides in the door each night doesn't get his coat off before he's handed a list — go find the shoes, go find the remote, go find out why dinner's late. Everyone in the house treats him like hired help with a wedding ring: that's the respectful title for someone's husband.
items.reading_mnemonic: ご stays ご, 主 gives しゅ, and 人 gives じん — stacked together they produce <reading>ごしゅじん</reading>.
items.description: This is the respectful term for someone else's husband, used when talking to or about the listener's family — not the word you'd use for your own husband. It leans on 主人 (master), so some speakers now avoid it for the gendered assumption baked in.

example_sentences.japanese: ご主人は今日、忙しいですか。

items.mnemonic_text: The one in the back rooms: okusan.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the very top of the mountain trail, a woman leans against the lone vending machine, patient in the shade of an oak, clearly waiting for somebody. Every exhausted hiker who finally staggers up assumes she must belong to whoever shows up gasping right after — and that assumption, someone waiting up there for her other half, is exactly (someone's) wife.
items.reading_mnemonic: She waves at the oak baking in the noon sun and calls down the trail, <reading>oak sun</reading> — the greeting that carries all the way to the switchbacks. That call is just how <reading>おくさん</reading> sounds: someone's wife, waiting patiently at the top for him to catch up.
items.description: 奥さん is the respectful way to refer to or address someone else's wife — never your own. It also gets used casually to address a married woman in general, but it is not what a man calls his own wife.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼の奥さんに会いました。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]の奥[おく]さんに会[あ]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達の奥さんが来ました。
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]の奥[おく]さんが来[き]ました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a man climbs the mossy steps every evening expecting to be first, and every evening his own wife is already there ahead of him, feeding the shrine cats without a word of announcement. He never has to ask where she is — she is simply, quietly, always a step ahead of him. That settled certainty is (my) wife.
items.reading_mnemonic: He calls up the steps, <reading>Sue, ma!</reading>, thinking he's found Grandma Kane — but it's his own wife who turns around, cat in her arms. That startled beat is the sound of <reading>つま</reading>: realizing, again, that his wife got there first.
items.description: 妻 is the plain, slightly formal way a man refers to his own wife when talking to other people — it is not a word used for someone else's wife, and not one he'd use calling out to her directly.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の妻は今忙しいです。

example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]は妻[つま]と公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a woman is washing laundry when her husband wades in fully dressed, chasing a sock that floated loose, soaking his only good shirt in the process. She doesn't even look up — of course that's who waded in after one sock, nobody else would bother. That reliable, faintly ridiculous devotion is (my) husband.
items.reading_mnemonic: He climbs out of the river dripping head to toe, sock triumphantly in hand, and she just sighs, <reading>Otto</reading>, not again — the exact sound of <reading>おっと</reading>, her name for the husband who always wades in after the laundry.
items.description: 夫 is the plain way a wife refers to her own husband when speaking to other people — not a word she'd use to call out to him directly, and not used for someone else's husband.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の夫は毎日忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: My husband is busy every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の夫[おっと]は毎[まい]日[にち]忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.english: I watch movies with my husband.
example_sentences.furigana: 夫[おっと]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.furigana: 夫[おっと]はコーヒーを飲[の]みます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: In Sei's school hallway, someone rounds the corner: just two legs mid-stride, a body carried along above them, heading forward without dragging anything else behind. Strip away every job title, every role, every name — what's left striding down that hallway is simply a <kanji>person</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a lone figure climbs the mossy steps at dusk, no name tag, just a shape moving past the cats. One cat swats at a bare foot and the figure yelps <reading>he-toe</reading>, which is exactly the sound of <reading>ひと</reading>, the word for person.

example_sentences.japanese: あの人は先生です。
example_sentences.furigana: あの人[ひと]は先[せん]生[せい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎日あの人と話します。
example_sentences.english: I talk with that person every day.

example_sentences.english: I meet a nice person at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]でいい人[ひと]に会[あ]います。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a stranger reaches for the last onigiri the exact moment you do. Neither of you lets go. You end up splitting it on the curb outside, silent and suspicious of each other, until one bite in you're both laughing about it — and just like that, you've made a friend.
items.reading_mnemonic: 友 gives とも and 達 gives だち, so stacked together they simply produce <reading>ともだち</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は友達と映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I watch a movie with my friend.

items.mnemonic_text: The one born before you in knowledge: sensei.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The legs that always stride out <kanji>ahead</kanji> of everyone reach the classroom first, plant themselves at the front, and refuse to sit down. Beneath their feet is the same patch of ground where a seed cracks open into <kanji>life</kanji> — because this is the one person whose ideas take root in you and grow. That's a teacher.
items.reading_mnemonic: 先 gives せん and 生 supplies the same せい you know from <reading>Sei</reading>, the star student — stack them together and you get exactly 「<reading>せんせい</reading>」.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は先生に聞きました。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は先[せん]生[せい]に聞[き]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: あの先生はいい人です。
example_sentences.english: That teacher is a good person.
example_sentences.furigana: あの先[せん]生[せい]はいい人[ひと]です。

items.mnemonic_text: One in the life of study: gakusei.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The child camped beneath that roof of scribbled notes refuses to go home, and overnight the desk starts to feel like part of them — that's daily <kanji>study</kanji>. But they're not finished growing: the same soil that turns a seed into <kanji>life</kanji> is still working underneath them, a person still half-sprouted, still becoming. That's a student.
items.reading_mnemonic: 学 gives がく and 生 supplies the same せい you already know from <reading>Sei</reading>, the star student, combining exactly into 「<reading>がくせい</reading>」.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は学生です。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は学[がく]生[せい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は学生ですか。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は学[がく]生[せい]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 学生は本を読みます。
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がく]生[せい]は本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same patch of earth where a seed splits open into <kanji>life</kanji> now stretches out as a schoolyard, planted with row after row of identical green shoots, all still too short to see over the fence. They're not finished yet — still rooted, still waiting their turn to grow — and that half-grown state is exactly what a pupil is.
items.reading_mnemonic: 生 gives せい and 徒 gives と, so stacked together they simply produce <reading>せいと</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 生徒は毎朝学校に行きます。
example_sentences.english: The pupils go to school every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 生[せい]徒[と]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A goldfish that stopped blinking gets carried into the clinic, though goldfish famously have no eyelids. The receptionist doesn't even look up — stranger visits happen weekly. When your name is finally called, the person in the white coat with a stethoscope swinging off one ear is exactly who you came for: the <kanji>doctor</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 医 gives い and 者 gives しゃ, so stacked together they simply produce <reading>いしゃ</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、医者に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I'm going to the doctor tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、医[い]者[しゃ]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 医者は今、忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: The doctor is busy right now.
example_sentences.furigana: 医[い]者[しゃ]は今[いま]、忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達と一緒に医者を待ちます。

example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に医[い]者[しゃ]を待[ま]ちます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every floor the elevator stops at, the same tired figure in a grey suit steps on, straightens a badge, staples one form, and steps off two floors later to do it all again. Nobody remembers his name, only his badge and his sigh. That endless loop of suit, badge, and paperwork is exactly what the word means: company employee.
items.reading_mnemonic: His badge, half-covered by his tie, reads <reading>Kai Shain</reading> in blocky letters — no one at the company can pronounce it right, but everyone recognizes that a <reading>かいしゃいん</reading> like him has been riding this elevator since it was installed.

example_sentences.japanese: 会社員の友達とお茶を飲みます。
example_sentences.english: I drink tea with my friend who's a company employee.
example_sentences.furigana: 会[かい]社[しゃ]員[いん]の友[とも]達[だち]とお茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、会社員の兄に会います。
example_sentences.english: Tomorrow I'm meeting my older brother, who's a company employee.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、会[かい]社[しゃ]員[いん]の兄[あに]に会[あ]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 母は会社員ではありません。
example_sentences.english: My mother is not a company employee.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は会[かい]社[しゃ]員[いん]ではありません。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning the galloping <kanji>station</kanji> horse thunders onto the platform, and it isn't the conductor who deals with it — it's the whistle-blowing worker in uniform who chases it back off the tracks before the first train arrives. Radio crackling, cap crooked, unbothered by any of this: that worn-out but unshaken figure is your station staff.
items.reading_mnemonic: Over the radio the worker's reply crackles back garbled, just an <reading>echo in</reading> the tunnel — but that crackly <reading>えきいん</reading> is on every platform of this line, herding lost passengers back before the doors slide shut.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅員に聞きます。
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]員[いん]に聞[き]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は駅員です。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は駅[えき]員[いん]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日駅員に会いました。
example_sentences.english: I met the station staff today.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Someone's been dumping fish traps along the riverbank at night, and every trap turns up empty by morning except the one time a figure in a sharp uniform wades in at dawn, hauls the traps out by hand, and confiscates the lot without a word. That quiet, uniformed figure standing ankle-deep in river mud is exactly what the word means: police officer.
items.reading_mnemonic: 警 gives けい and 官 gives かん, so stacked together they simply produce <reading>けいかん</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 公園で警官を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I saw a police officer at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]で警[けい]官[かん]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 警官が家に来ました。
example_sentences.english: A police officer came to the house.
example_sentences.furigana: 警[けい]官[かん]が家[いえ]に来[き]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、警官に会いました。
example_sentences.english: Yesterday I met a police officer.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、警[けい]官[かん]に会[あ]いました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Follow the <kanji>person</kanji> already mid-stride past the slanted gate, headed <kanji>outside</kanji> — but this time they don't stop at the fence. They keep walking until the walls that wrap an entire <kanji>country</kanji> shrink into a smudge on the mountain trail behind them. Striding clean outside your own country's walls is what makes you a foreigner.
items.reading_mnemonic: Each kanji keeps its taught reading in a row — 外（がい）＋国（こく）＋人（じん） — giving you <reading>がいこくじん</reading> straight down the line.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は外国人です。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は外[がい]国[こく]人[じん]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 外国人とお茶を飲みました。
example_sentences.english: I drank tea with a foreigner.
example_sentences.furigana: 外[がい]国[こく]人[じん]とお茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]みました。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日、公園で外国人に会いました。
example_sentences.english: Today I met a foreigner at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、公[こう]園[えん]で外[がい]国[こく]人[じん]に会[あ]いました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the kneeling <kanji>woman</kanji> finally rises from her bow and falls into step beside the two legs she already knows as a <kanji>person</kanji>, the pair of them striding together past the cats toward the enormous bell. Kneeling figure plus striding legs, moving as one down the mossy steps — that's a grown woman.
items.reading_mnemonic: 女 reads おんな and 人 reads ひと, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おんなのひと</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: あの女の人は医者です。
example_sentences.furigana: あの女[おんな]の人[ひと]は医[い]者[しゃ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は女の人と話します。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は女[おんな]の人[ひと]と話[はな]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 女の人が公園に行きます。
example_sentences.english: A woman is going to the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 女[おんな]の人[ひと]が公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Out in the paddy, the <kanji>man</kanji> finally straightens up from the plow, gives his arm one last flex, and starts walking toward Koichi's konbini for something cold — those two legs carrying him off the field are exactly the <kanji>person</kanji> he becomes the second he stops working. Power in the field, then legs on the road: that's a grown man.
items.reading_mnemonic: 男 reads おとこ and 人 reads ひと, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おとこのひと</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: この男の人は医者です。
example_sentences.furigana: この男[おとこ]の人[ひと]は医[い]者[しゃ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は男の人と話します。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は男[おとこ]の人[ひと]と話[はな]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 公園で男の人が待ちます。
example_sentences.english: A man will wait at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]で男[おとこ]の人[ひと]が待[ま]ちます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a tiny figure copies the kneeling <kanji>woman</kanji> pose out on the sports field, except her sweeping arm has curled inward to cradle a swaddled <kanji>child</kanji>, little arms flung out against her chest. A pint-sized woman who still has a bundled baby's shape tucked in her arms — that's a girl.
items.reading_mnemonic: 女 reads おんな and 子 reads こ, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おんなのこ</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: あの女の子は学生です。
example_sentences.english: That girl over there is a student.
example_sentences.furigana: あの女[おんな]の子[こ]は学[がく]生[せい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 女の子が公園で遊びます。
example_sentences.english: A girl plays in the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 女[おんな]の子[こ]が公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 女の子と一緒に映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I watch a movie with a girl.
example_sentences.furigana: 女[おんな]の子[こ]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Up on the mountain trail, a small figure flexes one arm at the vending machine exactly like the <kanji>man</kanji> dragging his plow through the paddy, except his other arm is still tucked into a <kanji>child</kanji>'s swaddle, wriggling loose at his side. A miniature man who hasn't finished unwrapping yet — that's a boy.
items.reading_mnemonic: 男 reads おとこ and 子 reads こ, so the two known readings simply chain together into <reading>おとこのこ</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: あの男の子は学生です。
example_sentences.english: That boy over there is a student.
example_sentences.furigana: あの男[おとこ]の子[こ]は学[がく]生[せい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 男の子が公園で遊びます。
example_sentences.english: The boy plays in the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 男[おとこ]の子[こ]が公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は男の子と話します。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は男[おとこ]の子[こ]と話[はな]します。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi points across the konbini at the kneeling <kanji>woman</kanji> restocking the onigiri shelf, arm sweeping the row into place. <kanji>He</kanji> doesn't explain, just tilts his head and grins: that's the one he's been talking about all week. You don't need more than that look to know she's his girlfriend, and now you know who she is too.
items.reading_mnemonic: 彼 gives かの and 女 gives じょ, so stacked together they simply produce <reading>かのじょ</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は本を読みます。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 僕は彼女と公園に行きます。

example_sentences.furigana: 僕[ぼく]は彼[かの]女[じょ]と公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は今忙しいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は今[いま]忙[いそが]しいです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, by the vending machine, a hiker's toddler drops her snack and wails so hard her whole face floods the same deep, angry <kanji>red</kanji> as the ground splitting open on that hillside, glowing from the fire underneath. Nothing quiets a face that red. That furious red-faced bundle is a baby.
items.reading_mnemonic: The reading is exactly the pieces you already know: 赤 gives you the あか, and the childish ちゃん suffix tacks straight on after it, spelling out <reading>あかちゃん</reading>.

example_sentences.english: There's a baby in the family.
example_sentences.furigana: 家[か]族[ぞく]に赤[あか]ちゃんがいます。

example_sentences.japanese: お母さんが赤ちゃんと遊びます。
example_sentences.furigana: お母[かあ]さんが赤[あか]ちゃんと遊[あそ]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 公園で赤ちゃんを見ます。
example_sentences.english: I see a baby at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]で赤[あか]ちゃんを見[み]ます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the tinny loudspeaker crackles once and a single voice booms through every aisle at the same instant, announcing a surprise scavenger hunt: onigiri, umbrellas, batteries, go. Every last customer looks up from what they're doing in the same second - not some of them, not most of them. Everyone.
items.reading_mnemonic: みんな is written exactly the way it sounds, plain kana with nothing hiding underneath, so the word simply is its own reading: <reading>みんな</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: みんなが公園で遊ぶ。
example_sentences.furigana: みんなが公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]ぶ。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達がみんなに話す。
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]がみんなに話[はな]す。

example_sentences.english: Tomorrow everyone is going to the sea together.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]みんなで海[うみ]に行[い]く。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The woodcutter is dividing the day's woodpile, and the sword is doing the arithmetic. Every log comes down into two leaning <kanji>parts</kanji>: one part for the village, one part he plants his boot on. The sword <kanji>understands</kanji> the rule immediately and never miscounts — the half with a boot on it is oneself.
items.reading_mnemonic: 自 gives じ and 分 gives ぶん, so stacked together they simply produce <reading>じぶん</reading>.
items.description: It points at whoever is speaking or being talked about, so it comes out as myself, yourself, or herself depending on the sentence. In casual speech it also works as a plain, slightly blunt word for I.

example_sentences.japanese: 自分で行きます。
example_sentences.furigana: 自[じ]分[ぶん]で行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 自分の部屋で寝ます。
example_sentences.english: I sleep in my own room.
example_sentences.furigana: 自[じ]分[ぶん]の部屋[へや]で寝[ね]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 自分で本を買いました。
example_sentences.furigana: 自[じ]分[ぶん]で本[ほん]を買[か]いました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: In the echoing hallway of Sei's school, gym class lets out and everyone crowds through one narrow doorway at once - shoulders, bags, elbows, all jammed together. Except one part always squeezes through first, out ahead of everything else, cutting a path for the rest of the body to follow: the head.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine keeps one badly behaved llama tied up by the great bell, and it despises every visitor who gets too close, so it swings and clonks them square in the skull. The caretaker just sighs and warns newcomers the same way each time: mind <reading>a llama</reading>, or it'll crack your <reading>あたま</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 猫の頭を見た。
example_sentences.english: I looked at the cat's head.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]の頭[あたま]を見[み]た。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の頭は寒い。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の頭[あたま]は寒[さむ]い。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は毎日頭を使う。
example_sentences.english: He uses his head every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は毎[まい]日[にち]頭[あたま]を使[つか]う。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat named Botan leaps onto the offering bowl and stares down at the water pooled inside it, hunting the strange animal staring back. It takes three tail-lashes before Botan realizes the intruder blinks whenever she blinks — it is her own face, staring up out of the water.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cow wanders into Grandma Kane's shrine and butts the shrine bell aside just to see what's cooking. The monk grabs the <reading>cow</reading> by the horns and yells right into its <reading>かお</reading> — but its blank face never changes.

example_sentences.japanese: 友達の顔を見ました。
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]の顔[かお]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 赤ちゃんの顔はいいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 赤[あか]ちゃんの顔[かお]はいいです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Above the register at Koichi's konbini hangs a security frame with two little dots for pupils, tilted so it looks like it's staring you down while you pick between the onigiri and the beeping till. That frame with pupils staring back is exactly the <kanji>eye</kanji> watching every customer who lingers too long.
items.reading_mnemonic: 目 already gives you this reading on its own — め is exactly how 目 reads by itself, so the <reading>め</reading> here is that very same reading, unchanged.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の目はいいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 医者は私の目を見ます。

example_sentences.furigana: 朝[あさ]、目[め]を開[あ]けます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Near the top of the mountain trail, that dangling flap of skin catches the sudden beep of the vending machine echoing off the rock face before your eyes even register the machine is there. The flap swivels toward the sound like it has a mind of its own — proof that the whole point of an <kanji>ear</kanji> is hearing first, seeing second.
items.reading_mnemonic: 耳 already reads みみ on its own, so the <reading>みみ</reading> in this word is that same reading, said once for the character and now doubled for the word.

example_sentences.furigana: 犬[いぬ]の耳[みみ]はいい。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a heron plants itself ankle-deep and points its long beak straight up, sniffing the air to check whether the water's too cold to cross before wading in. That beak does the one job it's built for — smelling out trouble first — which is exactly what a nose is for.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a new transfer student named Hannah presses her face to the cafeteria window, sniffing out the menu before anyone announces it. The other kids nickname her <reading>はな</reading> on the spot — that <reading>Hannah</reading>-nose never misses a smell, even through glass.

example_sentences.japanese: 犬の鼻はいい。
example_sentences.furigana: 犬[いぬ]の鼻[はな]はいい。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の鼻が寒い。

items.meaning_mnemonic: That open square is still hanging there mid-yawn, exactly as you left it — nothing has been drawn inside it, because nothing needs to be. A hole with nothing inside was already the whole idea: it's just a <kanji>mouth</kanji>, caught wide open and refusing to close until you've said the word for it.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer's mouth hangs open under the buzzing lights, coughing, insisting he caught the <reading>cooties</reading> from someone's open <reading>くち</reading>. Koichi shoos him out before the till starts beeping and restocks the onigiri.

example_sentences.japanese: 医者が私の口を見ます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the vending machine dispenses exactly one item that day: a single chipped tooth, still faintly rattling, ejected after the last hiker crunched down on a stone hidden inside their rice ball. Everyone just runs a tongue along their own teeth, checking for the gap where a tooth used to be.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the nurse lets out one flat sound every time a kid limps in clutching their jaw — a startled <reading>ha</reading>, stretched thin like a gasp with nowhere to go. That same deadpan <reading>は</reading> is the whole word: the sound she makes over a broken tooth is the reading for tooth itself.

example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の歯[は]はいいです。

example_sentences.furigana: 医[い]者[しゃ]は私[わたし]の歯[は]を見[み]ます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same <kanji>hand</kanji> is still hanging out mid-air, wrist and all, waiting for the shake nobody's ever finished. It doesn't close, it doesn't wave — it just stays there, open-palmed, being exactly the shape it always was. That patient, unshaken shape is the word for hand.
items.reading_mnemonic: Same kanji, same lesson: 手 already gave you two readings, and this word just borrows the plain <reading>て</reading> reading straight off it.

example_sentences.furigana: 手[て]でパンを食[た]べます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女の手を見ます。

example_sentences.english: My hands are cold right now.
example_sentences.furigana: 今[いま]、手[て]が寒[さむ]いです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Up on the mountain trail, that mouth-topped pair of stopped legs is moving again, planted step after step all the way to the vending machine at the top, still barking orders down at itself with every stride. Whatever plants itself like that and carries you onward — that's your <kanji>foot</kanji>, your leg.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a fisherman wades in and yelps <reading>ahh, sheesh</reading> as the icy water bites at his shins, hopping rock to rock on legs that won't go numb. By the fifth hop the whole riverbank knows the word for legs is <reading>あし</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 足で学校に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to school on foot.
example_sentences.furigana: 足[あし]で学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 猫の足を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I look at the cat's paws.

By closing, he's turned convenience-store scraps into an actual dish: cooking.

A disappointed hiker buys one anyway, shakes it like a maraca, and trudges back down still hungry: uncooked rice.

A chalkboard menu hangs from the mast, and the one waiter wades out in rubber boots to deliver plates. Tourists queue on the bank just to eat somewhere that technically counts as a restaurant, even though it's really a raft with silverware.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, past the lone vending machine, a hermit crab stops dragging its blistered shell. It wedges into a hollow rock at the trail's edge, lines up four pinecones in the doorway like doormats, and won't budge again. That hollow rock, doormats and all, is officially somebody's house — the crab has made itself a home.
items.reading_mnemonic: A builder named Ei nails one crooked wall onto that same hollow rock and steps back beaming, waiting for someone to ask about the roof. Instead he throws both arms up and shouts <reading>いえ</reading>, which lands on the ear exactly like an English <reading>yay</reading>, and declares the one wall a finished house.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every evening at Grandma Kane's shrine, the stray cats pile into one shivering heap on the mossy steps — not because any cat owns the place, but because the heap itself is the point. Ask an outsider cat to squeeze in and the whole pile hisses as one; ask one inside where home is, and it just presses closer. The heap is home.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is pure kana, spelled exactly the way it sounds, so <reading>うち</reading> needs no decoding — just read it as written.
items.description: うち means home in the sense of your own group or household, not just a building. Japanese speakers use it to mark insiders against outsiders, so it can describe a company, a team, or a family circle as easily as a physical house — a nuance the English word 'home' does not carry on its own.
