items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat that normally swats everything off the mossy steps stops mid-swat, sits down, and just stares at one stone lantern glowing gold in the evening light. Even the cranky, destructive cats agree on this one: it's lovely, it's wonderful, it's worth sitting still for.
items.reading_mnemonic: That same cat gets nicknamed <reading>sue-tech</reading>, because anything shiny short-circuits her, and she freezes at the lantern glow while everyone around her mutters <reading>すてき</reading> before she can even blink.

example_sentences.japanese: 素敵な映画を見ました。
example_sentences.furigana: 素[す]敵[てき]な映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: この部屋は素敵です。
example_sentences.furigana: この部屋[へや]は素[す]敵[てき]です。

example_sentences.japanese: あなたは素敵な人です。
example_sentences.furigana: あなたは素[す]敵[てき]な人[ひと]です。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Two teams line up on opposite banks of the river, rope pulled taut between them, boots dug into the mud, each side straining directly against the other's pull. Neither team gives an inch — that dead-even standoff, everyone pulling the opposite way from everyone else, is exactly the picture for opposite, against.
items.reading_mnemonic: The referee, nicknamed <reading>hun-tie</reading> because his necktie unravels every time he blows the whistle, screams <reading>はんたい</reading> whenever one team yanks in the exact opposite direction from the other.

example_sentences.japanese: 白の反対は黒です。
example_sentences.english: The opposite of white is black.
example_sentences.furigana: 白[しろ]の反[はん]対[たい]は黒[くろ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 僕はそれに反対です。
example_sentences.furigana: 僕[ぼく]はそれに反[はん]対[たい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達は一緒に行くことに反対した。
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]は一[いっ]緒[しょ]に行[い]くことに反[はん]対[たい]した。

items.mnemonic_text: Head off down the crossroads: iku.
items.meaning_mnemonic: That stick figure who's always mid-stride, the one who can never <kanji>go</kanji> two seconds without moving to the next place, finally shoulders a bag and walks straight out the door one morning. You watch the doorway swing shut behind them. That's the whole word: to go.
items.reading_mnemonic: It's simply the taught <reading>い</reading> reading of 行 that Koichi already uses, plus く, spelling out <reading>いく</reading> exactly as the kanji already taught you.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日学校に行きます。
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達と一緒に駅に行く。
example_sentences.english: I'm going to the station with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に駅[えき]に行[い]く。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日デパートに行きました。
example_sentences.english: I went to the department store today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]デパートに行[い]きました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the crossroads, the tree spots someone trudging up the mountain trail, footsore and ready to quit, and doesn't wait politely — it stretches a branch out like a beckoning arm and hauls them under its shade before they can even ask. That's the tree's whole personality: it never chases anyone anywhere, it only ever makes people <kanji>come</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The tree at the crossroads spots a straggler still dragging up the trail and calls out <reading>coo, roo</reading> until they finally give in and come sit in its shade — that giving-in is exactly <reading>くる</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 弟が午後来る。
example_sentences.english: My younger brother is coming in the afternoon.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]が午[ご]後[ご]来[く]る。

example_sentences.japanese: 猫がここへ来ます。
example_sentences.english: The cat is coming over here.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]がここへ来[き]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: いつ駅に来る？
example_sentences.english: When are you coming to the station?
example_sentences.furigana: いつ駅[えき]に来[く]る？

items.mnemonic_text: Sweep up and go home: kaeru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The same weary traveler from 帰's story finally reaches the little house, drops the walking stick on the step, and collapses through the door without even taking off his shoes. That homeward pull was never about the walking — it's the whole shape of <kanji>return</kanji>, and once it starts pulling, stopping halfway was never on offer.
items.reading_mnemonic: 帰 already supplies かえ here and る supplies る, so return home comes out as <reading>かえる</reading> — the same reading you learned for 帰, just running straight into the verb ending.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は今日早く帰る。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は今日[きょう]早[はや]く帰[かえ]る。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は六時に家に帰る。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は六[ろく]時[じ]に家[いえ]に帰[かえ]る。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日会社から帰る。
example_sentences.english: I come home from the office every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]会[かい]社[しゃ]から帰[かえ]る。

items.mnemonic_text: Take food to the mouth: taberu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini is closing, and the last customer ducks under the peaked tent-roof from 食's story — the shelter built entirely out of dinner, rice and side dishes heaped under the eaves. There's nothing else you can do under a roof like that but sit down where you're standing and <kanji>eat</kanji>, so that's exactly what closing time forces on him.
items.reading_mnemonic: 食 already gives た, べ gives べ, and る closes it out, so to eat becomes <reading>たべる</reading> exactly as those three pieces already spelled it.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎日ご飯を食べます。
example_sentences.english: I eat a meal every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]日[にち]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼はレストランで魚を食べました。
example_sentences.english: He ate fish at a restaurant.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]はレストランで魚[さかな]を食[た]べました。

example_sentences.japanese: 一緒に晩ご飯を食べましょう。
example_sentences.furigana: 一[いっ]緒[しょ]に晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べましょう。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, the food radical sits beside that same gaping, thirsty mouth from 飲's story, but now it's not just hanging open — it's tipped straight back over the water, gulping in one long pull. No plate ever touches those lips, only river water pouring straight down, and that greedy tilt-and-gulp is what it means to <kanji>drink</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a garden gnome missing from Koichi's konbini shelf washes up clutching an inner tube and a can. The fisherman hauling him in swears he gasped for a <reading>no-moo</reading>, exactly the sound of <reading>のむ</reading>, before sliding back under, still drinking.

example_sentences.japanese: 冷たい水を飲みます。
example_sentences.furigana: 冷[つめ]たい水[みず]を飲[の]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎朝コーヒーを飲みます。
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]朝[あさ]コーヒーを飲[の]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼はお酒を飲みました。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]はお酒[さけ]を飲[の]みました。

items.mnemonic_text: Eye on legs going to look: miru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The eye that stood up on legs is exhausted from all its walking, so it stops in the middle of the road and just stands there. It doesn't blink, doesn't turn away, doesn't do anything else at all — it just plants its legs and looks. That is all this word ever asks of you: to <kanji>see</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the guide Mia unpacks a cracked hand mirror instead of a map and holds it up to the sun, tilting it at hikers below. She calls down that all she needs is a <reading>mirror</reading>, the sound of <reading>みる</reading>, and spends the whole afternoon flashing light across the valley instead of guiding anyone up.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎日テレビを見ます。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]日[にち]テレビを見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日友達と映画を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I watched a movie with a friend yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 窓から山を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I look at the mountains from the window.
example_sentences.furigana: 窓[まど]から山[やま]を見[み]ます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit presses her ear against the gate of the shrine one more night, straining to catch the whispers behind it. But tonight she can't just stay quiet about it — she raps on the wood and demands to know what they're saying. Pressing an ear to a gate gets you two things: you listen, and eventually you have to <kanji>ask</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit giggles every time the wind <reading>kicks</reading> up, which is the only signal she needs to start <reading>きく</reading>ing at the gate again.

example_sentences.japanese: 毎朝ラジオを聞きます。
example_sentences.english: I listen to the radio every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]朝[あさ]ラジオを聞[き]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達に道を聞きます。
example_sentences.english: I ask a friend for directions.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]に道[みち]を聞[き]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 母の声を聞きました。
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]の声[こえ]を聞[き]きました。

items.mnemonic_text: Let the tongue tell it: hanasu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a mouth keeps releasing stacked lines of speech across the water, one slab after another, while right beside it a tongue wags nonstop, egging it on for more. Between the two of them the water is drowned out entirely — this is what it sounds like when someone won't stop <kanji>talking</kanji>. That endless back-and-forth is what it means to speak.
items.reading_mnemonic: Hana, a heron who wades the riverbank, opens her long beak and lets out a honk that sounds exactly like <reading>はな</reading>, then finishes it off with a brisk <reading>す</reading> snap of her bill — together that's <reading>はなす</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は先生と話します。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は先[せん]生[せい]と話[はな]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 僕は友達と話した。
example_sentences.furigana: 僕[ぼく]は友[とも]達[だち]と話[はな]した。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は学校で話しません。
example_sentences.english: She does not speak at school.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は学[がっ]校[こう]で話[はな]しません。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a stone mouth carved into the old bell pushes out one neat stacked layer of speech every time a cat brushes past it, like it's reading off a single fixed line it memorized decades ago. It never adds anything, never explains, it just delivers that one word again and again. That single fixed word, pushed out and done, is what it means to <kanji>say</kanji> something.
items.reading_mnemonic: Ichi the shrine cat only ever meows one clipped sound, a flat <reading>ee-oo</reading> that the cats around the bell have started imitating, and that sound is exactly <reading>いう</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女はこれが好きだと言います。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]はこれが好[す]きだと言[い]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は何と言いましたか。
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は何[なに]と言[い]いましたか。

example_sentences.japanese: 母はお茶を飲むと言いました。
example_sentences.english: My mother said she would drink tea.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]はお茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]むと言[い]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: Sell words to your eyes: yomu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini till goes quiet — the merchant has abandoned his onigiri shelf and is hunched over the register receipt instead, lips moving syllable by syllable down the tiny print. Wares untouched, eyes locked on the page, mouth shaping every line he isn't selling. That hunched, silent scanning is the whole picture of learning to <kanji>read</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: On Sei's school sports field, a cow named Yoko wanders in from nowhere and parks herself on the pitcher's mound with a paperback. Nobody can get her to move until she finishes the page, mooing a flat <reading>yo, moo</reading> at anyone who interrupts, which is exactly <reading>よむ</reading>, and refusing to budge until the chapter ends.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎朝新聞を読みます。
example_sentences.english: I read the newspaper every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]新[しん]聞[ぶん]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は図書館で本を読みます。
example_sentences.english: She reads books at the library.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 僕は今この本を読みます。
example_sentences.english: I'm going to read this book now.
example_sentences.furigana: 僕[ぼく]は今[いま]この本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every evening at your desk the sun sinks below your notebook exactly like it always does, and the instant its last light fades your hand starts moving on its own, filling line after line in the dark with no lamp to help. That daily blackout scribbling, repeated night after night, is the whole ritual of learning to <kanji>write</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Perched on the power line above Koichi's konbini, Kaa the crow burns through a stack of receipt paper with tiny flame-puffs, scorching every sheet into a <reading>khaki</reading> brown before it hits the ground. She calls the color <reading>かく</reading>, insists it counts as her handwriting, and refuses to use ink like everyone else.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は手紙を書きます。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は手[て]紙[がみ]を書[か]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 僕は毎朝ノートに書きます。
example_sentences.english: I write in my notebook every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 僕[ぼく]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]ノートに書[か]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は黒いペンで書きます。
example_sentences.english: The teacher writes with a black pen.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は黒[くろ]いペンで書[か]きます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You spot something you want and reach for the cowrie shell that's stood in for money since forever, laying it flat on the counter and sliding it across before you can lose your nerve. Shell handed over, prize now in your other hand — that whole exchange, shell for object, is exactly what it means to <kanji>buy</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 買 already gives you か, and the ending う stays う, spelling out <reading>かう</reading> exactly as taught.

example_sentences.japanese: 私はパンを買います。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はパンを買[か]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は新しいかばんを買う。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は新[あたら]しいかばんを買[か]う。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、スーパーで牛乳を買います。
example_sentences.english: Tomorrow I will buy milk at the supermarket.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、スーパーで牛[ぎゅう]乳[にゅう]を買[か]います。

items.mnemonic_text: Lay goods on the stand: uru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture that same street vendor leaning back on his two kicked-out legs, sign propped above his stacked goods, still shouting prices at everyone who walks past. He never once stops to hand over money himself — only to unload what's piled in front of him onto whoever stops. That relentless shouting-and-unloading is exactly what it means to <kanji>sell</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 売 already gives you う, and the ending る stays る, spelling out <reading>うる</reading> exactly as taught.

example_sentences.japanese: 母は古い服を売ります。
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は古[ふる]い服[ふく]を売[う]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は駅で新聞を売ります。
example_sentences.english: He sells newspapers at the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は駅[えき]で新[しん]聞[ぶん]を売[う]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: この店はパンを売りません。
example_sentences.english: This shop does not sell bread.
example_sentences.furigana: この店[みせ]はパンを売[う]りません。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every dawn, an old monk climbs Grandma Kane's mossy shrine steps at the exact same unhurried pace, one bell-toll per step, never rushing even when the temple cats race past him. Visitors say they could set their watches by him. That plodding, deliberate, one-foot-after-the-other pace up the steps is exactly what this word means: to walk.
items.reading_mnemonic: The tourists nickname the shrine monk 'the <reading>rook</reading>,' since like a chess rook he only ever creeps one square forward. Every morning the cats chant his rhythm up the mossy stairs: <reading>あるく</reading>, あるく, あるく, one slow step at a time.

example_sentences.japanese: 毎朝、駅まで歩きます。
example_sentences.english: I walk to the station every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]朝[あさ]、駅[えき]まで歩[ある]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達と公園を歩きました。
example_sentences.english: I walked through the park with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]と公[こう]園[えん]を歩[ある]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は家から学校まで歩く。
example_sentences.english: Today I walk from home to school.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は家[いえ]から学[がっ]校[こう]まで歩[ある]く。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Sei is already late for practice when the coach spots him at the classroom door. There's no time to warm up, so he just bolts, straight down the echoing hallway and out onto the sports field, arms pumping, shoes slapping tile and then grass. The coach doesn't even blink. That flat-out, no-warning sprint across the field is to run.
items.reading_mnemonic: As Sei rockets across the field, the announcer's shout comes out garbled through the loudspeaker — all anyone hears is <reading>ha-shee-roo</reading>, over and over, close enough to <reading>はしる</reading> that the whole team starts using it as their word for tearing across the grass.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎朝公園を走ります。
example_sentences.english: I run in the park every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]公[こう]園[えん]を走[はし]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は学校まで走りました。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は学[がっ]校[こう]まで走[はし]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、友達と駅まで走ります。
example_sentences.english: Tomorrow, I will run to the station with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、友[とも]達[だち]と駅[えき]まで走[はし]ります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi falls face-first into the river trying to grab a floating onigiri wrapper before it drifts past Grandma Kane's shrine steps. He can't touch the bottom, so he flails, arms churning, head barely above the current, refusing to let go of the wrapper. That desperate, arms-churning motion through water is to swim.
items.reading_mnemonic: Watching him thrash, the cats lined up on the shrine steps cheer him on with what sounds like <reading>oh-yo-go</reading>, as if urging 'oh, go, go!' — close enough to <reading>およぐ</reading> that Koichi adopts it as his own victory shout every time he drags himself back to shore.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎朝川で泳ぎます。
example_sentences.english: I swim in the river every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]川[かわ]で泳[およ]ぎます。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日、友達と海で泳ぎます。
example_sentences.english: Today I swim in the sea with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、友[とも]達[だち]と海[うみ]で泳[およ]ぎます。

example_sentences.japanese: 冬は海で泳ぎません。
example_sentences.english: I don't swim in the sea in winter.
example_sentences.furigana: 冬[ふゆ]は海[うみ]で泳[およ]ぎません。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, a cat sunning itself beside the vending machine is startled by a hiker's dropped can, and it doesn't just scurry off — it launches clean over the machine in one motion, all four paws leaving the ground at once. That single clean launch off the ground, whether across a gap or straight up, is to fly or jump.
items.reading_mnemonic: As the cat sails over the machine, it clips a tuba someone left leaning against it, and the horn lets out a low <reading>toh-buh</reading> honk mid-air — the exact sound the hikers now shout as <reading>とぶ</reading> every time that cat launches itself again.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の帽子が風で飛びます。
example_sentences.english: My hat blows away in the wind.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の帽[ぼう]子[し]が風[かぜ]で飛[と]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 大きい鳥が空を飛びます。
example_sentences.english: A big bird flies through the sky.
example_sentences.furigana: 大[おお]きい鳥[とり]が空[そら]を飛[と]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 子供がベッドで飛びます。
example_sentences.english: The child jumps on the bed.
example_sentences.furigana: 子[こ]供[ども]がベッドで飛[と]びます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You fell asleep leaning against the onigiri shelf at Koichi's konbini, and the till starts beeping nonstop over a jammed barcode. The noise won't quit, so you peel your eyes open, stagger upright, and blink at the fluorescent lights. That beeping is the whole story: to wake up, to get up.
items.reading_mnemonic: Oki the night clerk always oversleeps at Koichi's konbini. Every morning the manager shouts <reading>おきる</reading>, get up, and jangles the shutter key — <reading>oh, key</reading> — until Oki finally rolls off the floor and opens the store.

example_sentences.japanese: 毎朝七時に起きます。
example_sentences.english: I wake up at seven every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]朝[あさ]七[なな]時[じ]に起[お]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 弟はまだ起きません。
example_sentences.english: My younger brother isn't up yet.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]はまだ起[お]きません。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は早く起きた。
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は早[はや]く起[お]きた。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You've hiked all the way up to the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail, and the climb wrecks you completely. You slump down against its warm hum, eyes shutting before you even decide to rest, and don't move again until morning. That collapse against the machine is what it means: to sleep.
items.reading_mnemonic: A hiker called Near always collapses <reading>near</reading> the mountain vending machine, murmuring <reading>ねる</reading> before he even finishes sitting down, and by dawn he's still curled against its warm hum, dead to the world.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎晩早く寝ます。
example_sentences.english: I go to bed early every night.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]晩[ばん]早[はや]く寝[ね]ます。

Cats pile onto their laps and pin them there. That's exactly what it means to <kanji>sit</kanji> — plant yourself and stay.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You reach the top of the mountain trail expecting the vending machine, but the same <kanji>rest</kanji> person is still slumped against the tree, arms crossed, a note pinned to the bark reading back tomorrow. Everyone else keeps hiking past; this one has turned a five-minute breather into calling off the whole day. That is 休む: to rest, to take a day off.

He offers to send her home; she just points at the line forming outside and grabs another crate. Some people rest between shifts. She has never once learned how — she just works.

She isn't waiting for a practice or a friend to finish up — she's just studying, alone, until every problem on the page is solved.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one persistent cat has taken to shadowing her every move — copying exactly how she rings the enormous bell, sweeps the mossy steps, and bows twice before the altar. Nobody assigned it a lesson; it simply watched an expert long enough to learn from her, one gesture at a time.

Every dawn it edges closer to her heels, and by autumn the visitors swear the cat has started to <reading>ならう</reading> her exact bow.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the resident cat keeps hooking a paw around the base of the enormous bell, testing whether today is the day it tips. Grandma Kane never shouts. She crouches down and taps the stone beside it, over and over, every morning, until the cat starts copying the tap instead of shoving. Patient repetition until someone else can do it themselves — that is what it means to teach.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane repeats the tapping so many mornings that the cats start yowling it back at her, a flat little <reading>おしえる</reading>, oh-shee-eh-ru, and the tourists on the mossy steps swear it sounds exactly like <reading>oh, she'll</reading> — she'll keep doing this forever, patiently teaching.

items.mnemonic_text: Divide it and grasp it: wakaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A shrine cat drags a ball of string down the mossy steps so badly knotted that nobody can find an end to it. The woodcutter sets the whole mess on his block, and the sword comes down: the knot falls open in two leaning <kanji>parts</kanji>, and every loop inside is suddenly plain. Split a thing and you <kanji>understand</kanji> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Nothing new here: 分 keeps the わ you were taught, か and る just trail along behind it, and the verb reads <reading>わかる</reading>.
items.description: The thing understood takes the subject particle, not the object particle — English speakers reach for the object one for months. It stretches to knowing a fact or recognising a person, and on its own it does the work of got it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the vending machine at the summit restocks like magic — until you catch the delivery man radioing ahead to a friend at dawn. Once you've seen him do it, you can't pretend not to anymore; the secret clicks into place and stays there. That sudden, permanent click, the moment the secret becomes yours, is what it means to know something.
items.reading_mnemonic: A shrew has been staking out those delivery crates for weeks and finally works out that the truck always arrives at dawn. <reading>しる</reading>, it seems to squeak, sounding just like <reading>shrew</reading> — now it knows exactly when to dart in before the machine even opens.
items.description: 知る marks the moment something becomes known, not the ongoing state of knowing it — for an ongoing "I know," learners need the continuous て-form instead of this plain form standing alone.

items.mnemonic_text: Turn it over in the mind: kangaeru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school sports field, the visiting kangaroo mascot stops mid-hop and just stands there, chin dipped, replaying the coach's instructions before committing to a single bounce. It refuses to move again until it has turned the play over enough times to be sure. Working something out fully before acting on it is what it means to think something through.
items.reading_mnemonic: The mascot pauses so long that the crowd starts chanting <reading>かんがえる</reading>, kan-ga-eh-ru, which to the visiting parents sounds exactly like <reading>kangaroo</reading> — and it really is one, still working through the play call before it dares to jump.
items.description: 考える describes working through a problem step by step — reasoning, weighing, deciding — rather than a passing feeling or fleeting thought. Reach for this one when actual mental effort is involved.

items.mnemonic_text: A thought in the heart: omou.
items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail you stop dead at the vending machine that has no business being up there, staring at the buttons without pressing any of them for a full minute. Your friend asks what's wrong. Nothing's wrong, you say — you're not doing anything, you're just standing here working through what you think and feel about a can of hot coffee.

The only thing that comes out of your mouth in reply is <reading>おもう</reading> — that same flat, thinking exhale, an <reading>oh, moo</reading> for whatever's turning over in your head.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the new hire gets handed the entire onigiri shelf and told to have every position memorized by closing time. He stands under the fluorescent lights reciting shelf slots to himself, ignoring the beeping till, until the whole shelf is burned into his skull. That's what memorizing something for good actually takes.

By closing time the chant has worn a groove straight into his memory, and what's left in his mouth is <reading>おぼえる</reading> — the sound of an <reading>oh, bore, you</reading> repeated until it sticks.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one of the cats buries the spare bell clapper under the mossy steps, fully intending to dig it back up. It naps in the sun instead. items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a tadpole flops onto a lily pad and refuses to leave. It sits there so long its tail shrinks and legs sprout, and by sunset it hops off the pad a frog. Nobody ever catches the exact moment it happens — one thing just quietly turns into another. That quiet turning, tadpole into frog, is to become.

Nothing with legs, nothing that breathes, just an object taking up space. That plain, unmoving presence is to exist.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every evening at Grandma Kane's shrine, the last visitor leaves and the ancient gate groans on its hinges. The caretaker leans her whole weight into it until the two heavy halves meet with a dull clang, sealing the mossy steps off from the night and the cats out. That final clang is the meaning: to close.
items.reading_mnemonic: The caretaker's name is Shizu, and when she shimmers the bronze gate shut at dusk, the metal catches the last orange light and seems to glow all along its seam. She <reading>shimmers</reading> it closed every single night — say <reading>しめる</reading> and picture that glowing gate swinging to.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a broken keychain flashlight sits in the discount bin by the register until a bored customer clips two fresh batteries onto its back and thumbs the switch. The little bulb sputters, then catches, glowing steady in his hand. That double motion — snapping something onto a thing and waking it up — is the meaning: to turn on, to attach.
items.reading_mnemonic: つける is written in kana exactly as it sounds, with no kanji hiding underneath: <reading>つける</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 電気をつける。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the summit vending machine's fluorescent panel flickers and dies in a gust of wind at the exact moment a hiker rubs yesterday's chalk arrow off the rock beside it with his thumb. Bulb dark, chalk gone, both within the same breath of wind — that's the meaning: to turn off, to erase.
items.reading_mnemonic: The ranger who patrols the mountain trail is named Kesu, and hikers joke that wherever he walks, lights die and marks vanish behind him. Whisper <reading>けす</reading> and picture him snapping his equipment <reading>case</reading> shut — every switch he touches goes dark, every chalk line under his boot disappears.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the teacher stacks a mountain of ungraded homework by the door until the pile itself looks ready to <kanji>exit / leave</kanji> on its own. Rather than wait for that, she shoves the whole stack out into the hallway and drops a permission slip in the mailbox besides — anything that needs to go, she takes out and sends. That's the meaning: to take out, to send.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei, the fastest kid at school, <reading>dashes</reading> for the door the instant the bell rings, worksheets flying out of his open bag behind him. Teachers have started calling it his name for the move: <reading>だす</reading> — always mid-dash, always flinging something out as he goes.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, you forgot your umbrella and it's pouring. The priest keeps a bin of spares by the mossy steps and lets you take one, no questions, as long as you understand it's not a gift — you're borrowing it, and it goes back tomorrow.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one of the temple cats treats a fallen toy <reading>car</reading> like the greatest find ever, dragging it around all day — but by evening it always drops it back on the steps, because even a cat instinctively knows how to <reading>かりる</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, everyone forgets a pencil at some point, and there's always one kid by the window who has extras. She holds one out without a word, already expecting it back before the bell rings — that's exactly what it feels like to lend something.
items.reading_mnemonic: At school, Sei <reading>casts</reading> a glance at her spare pencil, then slides it across the desk to a friend who forgot theirs, saying '<reading>かす</reading>' — a quick loan she fully expects back by the end of class.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the till beeps and beeps at a customer already halfway out the door, arms full of onigiri he never scanned. The clerk has to haul him back by the collar before he'll dig out his wallet. Nobody leaves that counter until the beeping stops — you always have to pay.
items.reading_mnemonic: The clerk hauls him back by the collar, shouting that he'll <reading>haul</reading> him to the register himself if he has to. Coins finally hit the counter. The whole scrambling scene is <reading>はらう</reading> — to pay.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane sits on the mossy shrine steps with her hands folded, cats draped over her feet like she isn't going anywhere. Whatever she's expecting hasn't come yet, so she just sits, still as the bell beside her. That stillness, held on and on without complaint, is what it means to wait.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cat wanders up and tries to strike a <reading>match</reading> against the shrine bell, hoping to hurry things along, but Grandma Kane doesn't even blink. She's content to <reading>まつ</reading> as long as it takes.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Two people come around the same bend of the riverbank from opposite directions, both staring at the water instead of the path, and walk straight into each other. They stumble apart, startled, and there's nothing left to do but say hello. That collision, two people suddenly face to face, is what it means to meet.
items.reading_mnemonic: They collide so hard both yelp <reading>ow</reading> at once, then just stand there rubbing their foreheads and laughing. That startled little run-in by the river is <reading>あう</reading> — to meet.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a tiny torii gate stands guard in front of the lone vending machine. You duck your head low, just like the ducking figure who taught you to <kanji>enter</kanji>, and step through the narrow gate into the clearing — the machine already humming, waiting.
items.reading_mnemonic: 入 already gave you the reading はい, so adding plain る spells out 「<reading>はいる</reading>」 directly.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school the bell rings and the hallway fills instantly, everyone funneling toward the same doorway like those two stacked mountains finally toppling outward under their own height. There's no lingering once the peaks give way — the whole crowd is already <kanji>exit / leave</kanji>, headed out.
items.reading_mnemonic: This one's regular: 出 gives で and る just adds the ending, together spelling out <reading>でる</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school the whole class lines up for the field-trip bus, but one boy refuses to sit until he's counted every seat twice. The driver revs the engine, the line surges forward, and the boy finally hops aboard as the doors hiss shut behind him. That's what it means to ride, to board.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, the driver bellows one rule before the bus leaves: <reading>no rule</reading> about pushing. A boy who never listens hops on anyway, and the driver sighs, muttering <reading>のる</reading> under his breath as the doors close on him again.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, an old fisherman poles his boat back to shore, but his cat refuses to get off, digging its claws into the plank. He tips the boat until the cat has no choice, and it tumbles onto the mud with an offended yowl. That's the picture: reluctant, undignified, but off.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a mossy stone bridge arches over the carp pond, and an old monk crosses it every morning at the exact moment the bell tolls, timing his steps to the sound. One morning he pauses to feed the pond cats, forgets the bell, and has to hustle to cross before it stops ringing.
items.reading_mnemonic: The monk crossing the bridge is nicknamed <reading>Walter</reading> by the tourists, and Grandma Kane calls out <reading>わたる</reading> every morning to hurry him across the mossy stones before the bell finishes tolling.

Nobody steps forward, nobody says go — the instant the horn sounds, the race just begins on its own, runners lurching off before they've even decided to move. That's what beginning looks like when nothing and nobody has to make it happen.
items.reading_mnemonic: Hazy Maru raises the horn and bellows <reading>Ha, Jimmy, Maru!</reading> across the field before anyone can move, and the racers bolt not because he counted down but because his shout already sounded like the race starting itself: <reading>はじまる</reading>.

items.mnemonic_text: It comes to an end: owaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the mossy steps go quiet and the cats freeze mid-stretch the instant the enormous bell rings its last, sagging note. items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a raccoon refuses to wade in without stripping down first, peeling a mud-caked jacket off one shoulder at a time and flinging it onto a rock before dog-paddling across. Every animal downstream waits for the splash that means the jacket is finally off and the crossing has begun.
items.reading_mnemonic: That riverbank raccoon has a name — the other animals call her <reading>Newgoo</reading> for the sound her claws make peeling wet fabric, a slow squelch like <reading>ぬぐ</reading>. Every time she strips the muddy jacket off before diving in, she drags the sound out long and slow, and the name stuck.

It stands back up wearing a lily pad like a hat, holding a look of total dignity, as if nothing happened. That straight-faced dignity in total defeat is what gets you — you cannot help it, you laugh, then grin the whole walk home.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the curry machine glitches. Instead of dropping the packet into the bin like it does for everyone else in line, it swivels, hums, and fires a steaming pouch of curry straight into your hands — skipping every other customer, no request made, no line waited in. Nobody arranged it. Something simply gave itself to you.

items.description: This verb only works when the giving benefits you or your in-group — someone does something for your side. A different verb covers everyone else giving to a third party, so it's easy to reach for this one in the wrong direction as a beginner.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the sports field at Sei's school, a kid who's wiped out on the skateboard deck all week finally lands the trick clean in front of the whole class. The board goes still under their feet — quiet, no more falling, no more trying. It's not luck; they can do it now, and the trick itself is finished.

items.description: This word also functions as the potential form of the verb 'to do,' so it can mean either 'able to do something specific' or simply 'possible' depending on context. items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, hikers find one improbable vending machine that only accepts jokes — feed it a bad enough pun and it judges you before dispensing a drink. That single machine standing between you and relief, checking whether you measure up before it lets you pass, is exactly a test.
items.reading_mnemonic: テスト is a loanword from English "test", written and read exactly as it sounds: <reading>テスト</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A boy chains his own ankle to his desk every night in the school hallway, papers piling knee-deep, refusing to unlock the cuff until dawn. A pigeon roosts on his head and won't leave either, staring at the pages until they stop turning. Neither of them moves until every problem is solved — that grinding, chained-in effort is study.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every night before he chains himself down, the boy mutters the same quiet oath: '<reading>Ben, cue, oh</reading>, no distractions.' Said fast, it slides into <reading>べんきょう</reading> — the sound of him swearing himself back to the desk.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the lone vending machine doesn't dispense drinks anymore. Every button jams, spits out a folded riddle instead, and demands you solve it before it will even consider a refund. Hikers arrive thirsty and leave with an armful of only more of these — unanswered questions and problems, stacked one on top of the last.
items.reading_mnemonic: A sticker on the machine reads, in block letters: '<reading>MONDAY</reading> deliveries only — no drinks.' Grumbled enough times on the hike back down, that word wears smooth into <reading>もんだい</reading>, the exact sound of every problem the machine caused.

example_sentences.japanese: この問題に答えます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A fisherman at the riverbank refuses to reel in anything until the river tells him something back. He shouts a question at the current, waits, and eventually a smooth stone washes up at his boots with a single word scratched into it. He pockets the stone before he even looks at the fish — to him, that scratched stone is the answer.
items.reading_mnemonic: The fisherman is named Kota, and every time a stone washes up he reads the word aloud, then tacks on his own tic: '<reading>Kota, eh?</reading>' Said quickly on the riverbank, that slurs into <reading>こたえ</reading> — his own name fused with the answer he just fished out.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one particular cat never blinks — it just stares at whatever offering was left on the mossy steps, as if grading it. Visitors have taken to leaving notes asking the cat what it's thinking. It never answers, but everyone leaves convinced that unblinking stare carries the real point of the offering — its meaning.
items.reading_mnemonic: A girl named Emi visits the shrine daily just to ask that cat what its stare means. She never gets an answer, only ends up muttering her own name back at it — '<reading>Emi</reading>, me, again' — until the sound wears down to <reading>いみ</reading>, the word she's really been chasing all along.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The mouth is still stacking layers of speech, but this time it doesn't stop where a single sentence would end — it keeps piling layer on layer, far past what one thought needs. That endless stack of <kanji>say</kanji> becomes an entire language, and every layer in it, taken alone, is a word.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini awning juts out over the sidewalk to greet you before you're even through the door — that's <kanji>front</kanji>, the part that always meets you first. Duck under it and Koichi leans out to fill the gap over his mouth with the one word that was missing: his <kanji>name</kanji>. Front first, then the name.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the mountain trail's lone vending machine, every button is carved with dense, stroke-packed marks instead of pictures — no plain lines anywhere, just rows of intricate symbols crammed into a space built for a simple picture. Whatever you call that whole crowded family of written characters, this word is it: kanji.
items.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a general named <reading>Khan</reading> wades in to rinse his coat and plants a boot on a rock hidden under the current — he yelps a startled <reading>gee</reading> loud enough to scatter the herons. Khan's gee: <reading>かんじ</reading>, the word for the crowded characters on the sign he still can't read.

That rounded, curling script the coach just invented by accident is exactly what this word names: hiragana.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the exhausted night clerk restocks imported snacks and refuses to write in curves. Every foreign product label gets stamped out in blocky, straight-edged letters, like they were sliced with a paper cutter instead of drawn by hand. That sharp, angular script reserved just for foreign words is katakana.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a transfer student's mouth won't stop — one open mouth stacking speech on speech, then another mouth joining in, piling word after word into a whole <kanji>language</kanji>. But every syllable that tumbles out is rolled and foreign, all flat vowels and hard Rs the local kids can't place. That foreign stack of speech is English.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker who speaks nothing but English barks <reading>Hey, go!</reading> at the stragglers by the summit vending machine. His clipped accent squashes the shout into the very sound of <reading>えいご</reading>, and that's the reading that's stuck to English ever since.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the shrine steps, dawn breaks and the <kanji>sun</kanji> climbs straight through the gate's window bar, marking a fresh day. Beside it, the tree's origin line still points to the very <kanji>origin</kanji> everything grew from, pressed flat into an ancient book. Then mouths start chanting, stacking speech on speech into a whole <kanji>language</kanji>, spoken over that book, in the land where the sun began. That stacked, sun-born tongue is Japanese.

Villagers repeat the barked count until it blurs into one word, <reading>にほんご</reading>, and that's the reading that sticks whenever someone names the language.
