example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は映[えい]画[が]が好[す]きです。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、友達と映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: Tomorrow I'll watch a movie with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: その映画は面白かったです。
example_sentences.furigana: その映[えい]画[が]は面白[おもしろ]かったです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, a hiker collapses in front of the lone vending machine and won't take another step. Her friend starts humming, then breaks into a full song about the cold drinks waiting at the summit. By the second verse the hiker is back on her feet, still humming, powered entirely by the song.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the vending machine, her friend keeps saying <reading>you oughta</reading> sing along before every button press, until the hikers are chanting it back in rhythm — <reading>oughta</reading>, <reading>oughta</reading> — and the phrase warps into <reading>うた</reading>, the machine's tinny jingle playing the actual song.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女はいつも楽しい歌を歌います。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]はいつも楽[たの]しい歌[うた]を歌[うた]います。

example_sentences.japanese: この歌は好きですか。
example_sentences.furigana: この歌[うた]は好[す]きですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達と一緒に歌を歌いました。
example_sentences.english: I sang a song together with my friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に歌[うた]を歌[うた]いました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: In the echoing school hallway, someone taped up a drawing so bad the paper itself seems embarrassed to hold it. Every student who passes stops, tilts their head, and produces the exact same reaction — because what's supposed to be a horse has four legs, three ears, and no clear idea which end is which.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei stops in the hallway, squints at the taped-up drawing, and says only <reading>え</reading> — one flat syllable, the same sound as the English <reading>eh</reading> you'd give a joke that didn't land. Every classmate who passes does the same thing, the hallway filling with confused, one-note え's.

example_sentences.japanese: 娘は絵が好きです。
example_sentences.furigana: 娘[むすめ]は絵[え]が好[す]きです。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は部屋で絵を見ました。
example_sentences.english: He looked at a picture in the room.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は部屋[へや]で絵[え]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: この絵は古いです。
example_sentences.furigana: この絵[え]は古[ふる]いです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same mouth still hasn't stopped, and now its stories have an audience: the cats at Grandma Kane's shrine gather on the mossy steps every evening because one of them just won't quit <kanji>talking</kanji>, spinning fresh stories about a fish the size of the bell. Nobody's ever proven a word of it, but nobody leaves either.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every time the storytelling cat starts up again, Grandma Kane calls out from the steps, <reading>Hannah, she</reading> really said that? — and the phrase blurs into <reading>はなし</reading>, the very story the whole shrine has gathered on the mossy steps to hear.

example_sentences.japanese: 私はよく友達と話します。
example_sentences.english: I often talk with my friends.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はよく友[とも]達[だち]と話[はな]します。

example_sentences.japanese: その話は面白いですか？
example_sentences.furigana: その話[はなし]は面[おも]白[しろ]いですか？

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は昨日、面白い話をしました。
example_sentences.english: The teacher told an interesting story yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は昨日[きのう]、面[おも]白[しろ]い話[はなし]をしました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, one customer plants himself at the register and asks about every single item on the shelf — the onigiri's expiration, why the till beeps twice, whether the till itself has feelings. Koichi answers thirty of these before the line behind reaches the door, and there's no sign of them stopping.
items.reading_mnemonic: Watching them pile up, Koichi mutters to the next person in line, <reading>she's too much</reading> — and the words blur into <reading>しつもん</reading>, the very thing holding up his till: one more question, then another, then another.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は先生に質問しました。
example_sentences.english: I asked the teacher a question.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は先[せん]生[せい]に質[しつ]問[もん]しました。

example_sentences.japanese: その質問は難しいです。
example_sentences.furigana: その質[しつ]問[もん]は難[むずか]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は授業で質問をしました。
example_sentences.english: She asked a question during class.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]で質[しつ]問[もん]をしました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Momo, the konbini clerk, hates chaos. Every dropped umbrella, chipped mug, and lost sock that wanders onto her counter gets a paper tag and a spot on the shelf, no matter what it is. She never asks what it means or why it's there — a thing is a thing, and every thing gets labeled and shelved.
items.reading_mnemonic: Momo stamps each tag with a flat moan: "moooono." Customers assume she's exhausted, but it's just her filing chant — one long <reading>moan</reading> for every <reading>もの</reading> she catalogs, thing after thing after thing.

example_sentences.japanese: これは私の物です。
example_sentences.furigana: これは私[わたし]の物[もの]です。

example_sentences.japanese: その箱の物は何ですか。
example_sentences.english: What are the things in that box?
example_sentences.furigana: その箱[はこ]の物[もの]は何[なに]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: その物を取ってください。
example_sentences.furigana: その物[もの]を取[と]ってください。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the gossip cat drags in a folded cot every evening and refuses to say a word until you're sitting on it. Only then does she report the day's matters — who fought, who left an offering, what toppled off the shelf — never a solid object you could hold, only something that happened.
items.reading_mnemonic: Every night the cat pats the cot twice before she'll talk, announcing the news with a soft double knock: "<reading>こと</reading>, <reading>こと</reading>" — the same sound as tapping a <reading>cot</reading>, her signal that a matter is about to be reported.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の言う事を聞いてください。
example_sentences.english: Please listen to what I say.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の言[い]う事[こと]を聞[き]いてください。

example_sentences.japanese: それは面白い事ですね。
example_sentences.english: That's an interesting thing, isn't it.
example_sentences.furigana: それは面[おも]白[しろ]い事[こと]ですね。

example_sentences.japanese: 好きな事をしました。
example_sentences.furigana: 好[す]きな事[こと]をしました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, past the lone vending machine, a toucan named Toco stubs her toe on the exact same rock every single hike. She stops, taps it twice, and declares that spot the place — not the trail, not the view, just the one stubbed patch of ground she keeps returning to.
items.reading_mnemonic: Toco's toe finds the same rock every hike, and she barks out her toe-corral: <reading>ところ</reading> — <reading>toe-corral</reading> — the small fenced-in place at the top of the trail that belongs only to her stubbed toe.

example_sentences.japanese: ここは静かな所です。
example_sentences.furigana: ここは静[しず]かな所[ところ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は静かな所が好きです。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は静[しず]かな所[ところ]が好[す]きです。

example_sentences.japanese: あそこは有名な所です。
example_sentences.english: That place over there is famous.
example_sentences.furigana: あそこは有[ゆう]名[めい]な所[ところ]です。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a fisherman raises his hoe like a compass whenever someone asks which way to wade across. He never points with his hand — only the hoe, tilted toward whichever direction the current looks calmest that day — and that single tilt is the only answer anyone gets.
items.reading_mnemonic: He grunts one flat <reading>ほう</reading> as the hoe swings — the same clipped sound as saying <reading>hoe</reading> with your mouth barely open — and that grunt-and-tilt is the whole direction anyone needs at the crossing.

example_sentences.japanese: すみません、駅はどちらの方ですか。
example_sentences.english: Excuse me, which way is the station?
example_sentences.furigana: すみません、駅[えき]はどちらの方[ほう]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 郵便局はあちらの方です。
example_sentences.english: The post office is that way.
example_sentences.furigana: 郵[ゆう]便[びん]局[きょく]はあちらの方[ほう]です。

example_sentences.japanese: こちらの方が近いです。
example_sentences.furigana: こちらの方[ほう]が近[ちか]いです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A customs officer refuses to ever say the word "person" — it's beneath the dignity of his line. Instead he stamps each passport with a flourish and announces "next, esteemed guest," bowing a fraction lower for the elderly and exactly the same for everyone else. That stiff, formal way of naming someone is the word itself.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a tailor sets up shop by the onigiri shelf, snipping fabric with a huge <reading>cutter</reading>. Every customer who walks in gets bowed to and called "esteemed <reading>かた</reading>" before he measures their shoulders for a suit nobody asked for.
items.description: As "person," 方 is a polite, formal register word — used to respectfully describe someone else (a customer, a stranger, an elder), not to refer to yourself or to talk casually about friends.

example_sentences.japanese: あの方は先生です。
example_sentences.english: That person over there is a teacher.
example_sentences.furigana: あの方[ほう]は先[せん]生[せい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: この方は誰ですか。
example_sentences.furigana: この方[ほう]は誰[だれ]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: その方はとても親切でした。
example_sentences.furigana: その方[ほう]はとても親[しん]切[せつ]でした。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You already know the gate with its two doors thrown open, the sun hanging low and trapped in the gap between them. Now a duck waddles up to that same gate and refuses to pass — it just paces back and forth in the strip of light, unwilling to leave the <kanji>interval / between</kanji> the two doors. That pacing, caught-in-the-middle strip of light is the word: an interval, the between.
items.reading_mnemonic: 間 already gives you the reading directly — the same one from the kanji's own gate-and-sun story, so 「<reading>あいだ</reading>」 is simply what you say.

example_sentences.japanese: 授業の間、静かに座っていました。
example_sentences.furigana: 授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]の間[あいだ]、静[しず]かに座[すわ]っていました。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達を待っている間に、コーヒーを飲みました。
example_sentences.english: While I was waiting for my friend, I drank some coffee.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]を待[ま]っている間[あいだ]に、コーヒーを飲[の]みました。

example_sentences.japanese: 朝と晩の間に、宿題をしました。
example_sentences.english: I did my homework sometime between morning and evening.
example_sentences.furigana: 朝[あさ]と晩[ばん]の間[あいだ]に、宿[しゅく]題[だい]をしました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker climbs the mountain trail for hours, certain the summit is impossibly far, only to trip over the vending machine at the top and realize it's the same one he passed at the trailhead. He'd walked in a circle the whole time. Whatever he'd been trudging toward was nearby the entire climb — he just never looked over his shoulder.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a <reading>cheeky cook</reading> has set up a stall serving free noodles to anyone who insists the summit is <reading>ちかく</reading> — nearby — even though they've clearly been climbing for hours. He never corrects them; free noodles for the delusional.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の近くに図書館があります。
example_sentences.english: There's a library near the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の近[ちか]くに図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]があります。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の家はこの近くです。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の家[いえ]はこの近[ちか]くです。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は公園の近くに住んでいます。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は公[こう]園[えん]の近[ちか]くに住[す]んでいます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one cat claims the mossy step by the bell, and a second cat — never asked, never invited — plants itself immediately beside the first, close enough their tails touch. Every single day it's the same two steps, side by side, the second cat permanently attached to whichever step the first one picks. That fixed, right-beside-you position is what the word means.
items.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>tawny</reading> cat has taken over the step <reading>となり</reading> — right next to — the shrine bell, and hisses at anyone else who tries to sit there, as if the neighboring step belongs to it alone.

example_sentences.japanese: 隣に猫がいます。
example_sentences.english: There's a cat next to me.
example_sentences.furigana: 隣[となり]に猫[ねこ]がいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 隣の部屋は静かです。
example_sentences.english: The room next door is quiet.
example_sentences.furigana: 隣[となり]の部屋[へや]は静[しず]かです。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の隣に座ってください。
example_sentences.english: Please sit down next to me.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の隣[となり]に座[すわ]ってください。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The runner is still frozen mid-stride, string trailing off his heel from a race that never seems to end. Now picture the whole pack has finished and gone home, and he's still out on the empty course, a few permanent steps back from where everyone else stood. That's his spot for good — <kanji>behind</kanji> the group, always trailing after.
items.reading_mnemonic: An <reading>usher</reading> at Sei's school assembly grabs every latecomer at the door, and instead of the empty front seats, walks them all the way to the back — <reading>うしろ</reading> — where they stand behind the whole crowd for the rest of the ceremony.

example_sentences.japanese: 後ろに猫がいます。
example_sentences.furigana: 後[うし]ろに猫[ねこ]がいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は私の後ろに立ちました。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は私[わたし]の後[うし]ろに立[た]ちました。

example_sentences.japanese: かばんは椅子の後ろにありました。
example_sentences.english: The bag was behind the chair.
example_sentences.furigana: かばんは椅[い]子[す]の後[うし]ろにありました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture that storefront awning again, jutting out over the sidewalk with its two-legged display stand planted beneath it. It's built to be the very first thing anyone sees, standing out in <kanji>front</kanji> of the shop, met <kanji>before</kanji> a single customer crosses the threshold. Whatever greets you first, whatever juts out ahead of everything else, is the front — the before.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word just carries over the kanji's own reading: 前 is read <reading>まえ</reading>, exactly as already taught.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の前でともだちを待ちます。
example_sentences.english: I'll wait for my friend in front of the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の前[まえ]でともだちを待[ま]ちます。

example_sentences.japanese: 食事の前に手を洗います。
example_sentences.english: I wash my hands before meals.
example_sentences.furigana: 食[しょく]事[じ]の前[まえ]に手[て]を洗[あら]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 三日前、私はこの町に来ました。
example_sentences.english: Three days ago, I came to this town.
example_sentences.furigana: 三[みっ]日[か]前[まえ]、私[わたし]はこの町[まち]に来[き]ました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The spear is still lodged dead center in that open square, exactly where you first pictured it — but now imagine trying to yank it back out and finding the square won't let go, gripping tight around the blade buried in its <kanji>middle</kanji>. Whatever's skewered that way isn't sitting near an edge; it's held fast, tucked <kanji>inside</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 中 keeps the reading you already learned for it: <reading>なか</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 箱の中に猫がいます。
example_sentences.english: There's a cat inside the box.
example_sentences.furigana: 箱[はこ]の中[なか]に猫[ねこ]がいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 部屋の中は暗かったです。
example_sentences.english: The inside of the room was dark.
example_sentences.furigana: 部屋[へや]の中[なか]は暗[くら]かったです。

example_sentences.japanese: かばんの中に財布がありました。
example_sentences.english: There was a wallet inside the bag.
example_sentences.furigana: かばんの中[なか]に財[さい]布[ふ]がありました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same figure is still at the slanted gate, one foot already past the threshold — but now picture them finally committing, both feet clearing the fence, the gate swinging shut behind them for good. Whatever was inside is someone else's problem now; they're standing in the open air, fully and firmly <kanji>outside</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 外 is read <reading>そと</reading>, exactly the reading already taught for this kanji.

example_sentences.japanese: 外は寒いです。
example_sentences.furigana: 外[そと]は寒[さむ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 犬は外にいます。
example_sentences.furigana: 犬[いぬ]は外[そと]にいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 外で遊びましょう。
example_sentences.furigana: 外[そと]で遊[あそ]びましょう。

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a goat drags the vending machine past the summit, still climbing — its hooves pointing the same way as that little mark rising off the ground: skyward. It won't stop until there's nothing left <kanji>above</kanji> it but open sky, which is exactly <kanji>up</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The word takes exactly the reading you already know from the kanji itself: 上 is read <reading>うえ</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 本は机の上にあります。
example_sentences.english: The book is on the desk.
example_sentences.furigana: 本[ほん]は机[つくえ]の上[うえ]にあります。

example_sentences.japanese: 猫は木の上にいます。
example_sentences.english: The cat is up in the tree.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]は木[き]の上[うえ]にいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 山の上は寒いです。
example_sentences.english: It's cold at the top of the mountain.
example_sentences.furigana: 山[やま]の上[うえ]は寒[さむ]いです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, someone balances a shelf mid-air while doing the laundry, and the little mark dangling off underneath it stops waiting — it drops, plop, straight into the current. Everything about that shelf still leans toward the space it fell from: <kanji>down</kanji>, <kanji>below</kanji> the surface, gone.
items.reading_mnemonic: The word takes exactly the reading you already know from the kanji itself: 下 is read <reading>した</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 猫はテーブルの下で寝ています。
example_sentences.english: The cat is sleeping under the table.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]はテーブルの下[した]で寝[ね]ています。

example_sentences.japanese: 財布を椅子の下で見つけました。
example_sentences.english: I found my wallet under the chair.
example_sentences.furigana: 財[さい]布[ふ]を椅[い]子[す]の下[した]で見[み]つけました。

example_sentences.japanese: 山の下に川があります。
example_sentences.english: There is a river below the mountain.
example_sentences.furigana: 山[やま]の下[した]に川[かわ]があります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer jams an arm into the vending slot up to the elbow, fishing after a stuck onigiri — the same fingers-into-open-mouth shape as before, working itself free all over again. It's always the dominant one doing this kind of stunt, which is why that grabbing hand is the <kanji>right</kanji> one.
items.reading_mnemonic: The word takes exactly the reading you already know from the kanji itself: 右 is read <reading>みぎ</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 銀行は右にあります。
example_sentences.english: The bank is on the right.
example_sentences.furigana: 銀[ぎん]行[こう]は右[みぎ]にあります。

example_sentences.japanese: 右の目が痛いです。
example_sentences.furigana: 右[みぎ]の目[め]が痛[いた]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: あの角を右に曲がってください。
example_sentences.english: Please turn right at that corner.
example_sentences.furigana: あの角[かど]を右[みぎ]に曲[ま]がってください。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, in the middle of shop class, someone braces a carpenter's square hard against a plank so it won't slip while a friend saws — the same tensed grip as before, the arm that isn't doing the cutting. That steadying arm is always the one on the <kanji>left</kanji>, holding everything still so the other hand can work.
items.reading_mnemonic: The word takes exactly the reading you already know from the kanji itself: 左 is read <reading>ひだり</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は角で左に曲がりました。
example_sentences.english: He turned left at the corner.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は角[かど]で左[ひだり]に曲[ま]がりました。

example_sentences.japanese: 銀行はデパートの左にあります。
example_sentences.english: The bank is to the left of the department store.
example_sentences.furigana: 銀[ぎん]行[こう]はデパートの左[ひだり]にあります。

example_sentences.japanese: 左の目が痛いです。
example_sentences.furigana: 左[ひだり]の目[め]が痛[いた]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: Backs turned to the cold: kita.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The two figures are still on that frozen bench, spine to spine, too stubborn to face the wind. A postman trudges by and asks which way is <kanji>north</kanji>. Neither turns around — they just jab a thumb back over the shoulder, into the gale that's been freezing them all along, and that's your answer.
items.reading_mnemonic: 北 already gives you this exact sound for the place name, so you just say <reading>きた</reading> straight from what you learned.

example_sentences.japanese: 北にコンビニがあります。
example_sentences.english: There's a convenience store to the north.
example_sentences.furigana: 北[きた]にコンビニがあります。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の家は北にあります。
example_sentences.english: My house is to the north.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の家[いえ]は北[きた]にあります。

example_sentences.japanese: 北の方に大きい山があります。
example_sentences.english: There's a big mountain to the north.
example_sentences.furigana: 北[きた]の方[ほう]に大[おお]きい山[やま]があります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: That tent is still pitched with its wind chime jingling under the roof, planted on the sunniest patch of ground you could find. You keep dragging the stakes further and further along, chasing the warmth, until the chime is going nonstop in the soft breeze — and dragging a tent that far only points one way: <kanji>south</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 南 already carries this reading for the place name, so that's the sound you use here too: <reading>みなみ</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 鳥は南へ飛びます。
example_sentences.furigana: 鳥[とり]は南[みなみ]へ飛[と]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 南はあちらです。
example_sentences.furigana: 南[みなみ]はあちらです。

example_sentences.japanese: 冬でも南は暖かいです。
example_sentences.english: Even in winter, the south is warm.
example_sentences.furigana: 冬[ふゆ]でも南[みなみ]は暖[あたた]かいです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning that same tree at the horizon snags the sun in its branches again, right on schedule. You watch it happen daily: the sun claws its way through the tangle, breaks free, and you know exactly which direction you're facing when it does — <kanji>east</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 東 already gives you this exact word's sound, so you just say <reading>ひがし</reading> straight from what you learned.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の家は駅の東にあります。
example_sentences.english: My house is east of the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の家[いえ]は駅[えき]の東[ひがし]にあります。

example_sentences.japanese: あの山は東にあります。
example_sentences.english: That mountain is to the east.
example_sentences.furigana: あの山[やま]は東[ひがし]にあります。

example_sentences.japanese: 東の空に月が見えます。
example_sentences.english: The moon can be seen in the eastern sky.
example_sentences.furigana: 東[ひがし]の空[そら]に月[つき]が見[み]えます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every dusk that squat cage fills up again, wings folding in one after another as the birds settle for the night. You count them home each time the sun dips the exact same direction, and that direction is always <kanji>west</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: 西 already carries this reading for the place name, so that's exactly what carries over here: <reading>にし</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅は西にあります。
example_sentences.english: The station is to the west.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]は西[にし]にあります。

example_sentences.japanese: 私たちは西へ歩きました。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]たちは西[にし]へ歩[ある]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 山は西のほうにあります。
example_sentences.english: The mountain is in the western direction.
example_sentences.furigana: 山[やま]は西[にし]のほうにあります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Han the half-and-half chef cleaves the crossed matchsticks down the middle, one perfect <kanji>half</kanji> either side of the beeping till. The woodcutter, unimpressed, sets a log by the onigiri shelf and drops it into two leaning <kanji>parts</kanji>. Two men, two clean cuts, and the konbini floor is nothing but half.
items.reading_mnemonic: 半 gives its はん and 分 its ぶん with no surprises, so the word is simply <reading>はんぶん</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: パンの半分を食べました。
example_sentences.english: I ate half of the bread.
example_sentences.furigana: パンの半[はん]分[ぶん]を食[た]べました。

example_sentences.japanese: 半分は私の物です。
example_sentences.furigana: 半[はん]分[ぶん]は私[わたし]の物[もの]です。

example_sentences.japanese: お金の半分を弟にあげました。
example_sentences.english: I gave half the money to my younger brother.
example_sentences.furigana: お金[かね]の半[はん]分[ぶん]を弟[おとうと]にあげました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the new monk doesn't leave one coin behind. He tips the entire offering box onto the mossy steps, sweeps every last piece into his sack, and pats the empty box twice to prove it: nothing remains inside. He took the whole thing, every part of it — that's the idea.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine keeps a monk on offering duty, and he only has one rule, chanted at every visitor: <reading>Zen-boo</reading> — give it all. He turns the donation box completely upside down and shakes it until the last coin drops. That chant is <reading>ぜんぶ</reading>, and it means the whole thing, nothing left inside.

example_sentences.japanese: この本を全部読みました。
example_sentences.furigana: この本[ほん]を全[ぜん]部[ぶ]読[よ]みました。

example_sentences.japanese: お金を全部使いました。
example_sentences.english: I used up all my money.
example_sentences.furigana: お金[かね]を全[ぜん]部[ぶ]使[つか]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 全部おいしかったです。
example_sentences.furigana: 全[ぜん]部[ぶ]おいしかったです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini restocks the onigiri shelf every morning, but today the delivery truck backs up too far and dumps three times the usual order. Onigiri spill off the shelf, stack on the floor, and pile up by the register until Koichi can't see the counter anymore. Customers wade through rice triangles just to check out — that's not a stocking error, that's a lot.
items.reading_mnemonic: たくさん is written exactly the way it sounds, kana only, nothing to decode: <reading>たくさん</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は本をたくさん買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a lot of books.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は本[ほん]をたくさん買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 公園に猫がたくさんいます。
example_sentences.english: There are a lot of cats in the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]に猫[ねこ]がたくさんいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は宿題がたくさんあります。
example_sentences.english: There's a lot of homework today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は宿[しゅく]題[だい]がたくさんあります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You've already watched someone take a bite out of small: slice one more dot off that hooked little shape and next to nothing survives. Pinch what's left between two fingers — that scrap, that residue, the near-nothing you can still hold onto — is exactly <kanji>few</kanji>. A little is whatever remains after almost everything else is gone.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sho, the tiny stage magician, never asks the crowd for much. Before every trick he holds up one white-gloved finger and requests just <reading>a skosh</reading> of hush, a skosh of powder, a skosh of anything at all. That signature request is <reading>すこし</reading> — a little, exactly his size, never more.

example_sentences.japanese: 水を少し飲みました。
example_sentences.furigana: 水[みず]を少[すこ]し飲[の]みました。

example_sentences.japanese: このコーヒーは少し熱いです。
example_sentences.english: This coffee is a little hot.
example_sentences.furigana: このコーヒーは少[すこ]し熱[あつ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 少し休みます。
example_sentences.furigana: 少[すこ]し休[やす]みます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer asks to sample every rice ball on the shelf before buying one, but takes only the tiniest sliver off the corner of each — never a real bite, just a taste. The clerk restocks behind him without noticing anything's missing. That's the whole trick of asking for just a little: barely there, gone before you'd call it a bite.
items.reading_mnemonic: This word is spelled in kana exactly as it's read, with no kanji to decode: <reading>ちょっと</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: ちょっと待って。
example_sentences.furigana: ちょっと待[ま]って。

example_sentences.japanese: このコーヒーはちょっと熱いです。
example_sentences.english: This coffee is a bit hot.
example_sentences.furigana: このコーヒーはちょっと熱[あつ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日はちょっと忙しいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]はちょっと忙[いそが]しいです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, one umbrella turns up in the lost and found every rainy week, and every student swears, straight-faced, that it belongs to someone else — never mine, always another person's. By the end of term nobody remembers whose it actually was, just an endless chain of pointing at whoever's standing nearby. That endless deflection is the word: other.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a peddler named Hoka the hawker never sells you anything from his own cart — he waves you further up the path, insisting you buy from the other hawker instead. Every climber ends up chasing an <reading>hoka</reading> who doesn't exist. His name says it plain: <reading>ほか</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 他の色はありますか。
example_sentences.english: Do you have this in another color?
example_sentences.furigana: 他[ほか]の色[いろ]はありますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 他の店で買います。
example_sentences.english: I'll buy it at a different shop.
example_sentences.furigana: 他[ほか]の店[みせ]で買[か]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 他の人に聞きます。
example_sentences.furigana: 他[ほか]の人[ひと]に聞[き]きます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, two cats that look identical fight nonstop, so she builds a low wall down the middle of the mossy steps just to keep them apart — one bowl on each side, one nap spot on each side, one bell on each side. Everything about their lives gets divided into its own separate portion, one and then another entirely. That's the word.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the shrine, one cat named Betsy refuses to share the steps with the others — she claims her own patch of moss, apart from every cat there, hissing if anyone crosses the line. Grandma just shrugs and calls her the <reading>べつ</reading> cat, plain as the sound of her own name: <reading>Betsy</reading> stays separate, always.

example_sentences.japanese: これは別の本です。
example_sentences.furigana: これは別[べつ]の本[ほん]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 別の店で靴を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought shoes at a different shop.
example_sentences.furigana: 別[べつ]の店[みせ]で靴[くつ]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 弟の部屋は別です。
example_sentences.english: My younger brother's room is separate.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]の部屋[へや]は別[べつ]です。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Someone collapses on the school sports field, forehead burning, and the same swirling wisp you've seen rise off a hot bowl of rice now curls up off their skin instead — their <kanji>spirit</kanji> visibly leaking out into the air with every ragged breath. The nurse takes one look at that steam and doesn't even need to ask what's wrong: illness.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kiki the tree spirit catches a chill on the mountain trail, and her usual giggle turns into a rasping cough that shudders through the branches, ending in a weak, wheezy <reading>b'yo-key</reading> sound — <reading>びょうき</reading> — the same puff of spirit as always, just worn thin by illness.

example_sentences.japanese: 父は病気で病院にいます。
example_sentences.english: My father is sick and he's at the hospital.
example_sentences.furigana: 父[ちち]は病[びょう]気[き]で病[びょう]院[いん]にいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は病気で仕事を休みました。
example_sentences.english: He was sick, so he took the day off work.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は病[びょう]気[き]で仕[し]事[ごと]を休[やす]みました。

example_sentences.japanese: 病気の人は医者に会います。
example_sentences.english: A sick person goes to see a doctor.
example_sentences.furigana: 病[びょう]気[き]の人[ひと]は医[い]者[しゃ]に会[あ]います。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Sei collapses face-down on the school field after the last sprint of practice, soaked in sweat. A cold wind knifes across the grass the instant she stops moving, and by evening she's shivering under three blankets with a raw throat and a fever — a cold caught in one gust of wind.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei's coach wraps her scraped knee in gauze at the edge of the field, and the wind — <reading>かぜ</reading> — snatches the loose end and flaps it like a flag. She hisses '<reading>gauze</reading>' through her teeth, kaze, the same wind that left her sick the next morning.
items.description: 風邪 is written with the same character as 風, 'wind' — colds were traditionally believed to be carried in on a bad wind, which is also why the everyday expression for catching a cold literally means 'to be hit by wind.'

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は風邪で学校を休みました。
example_sentences.english: She was absent from school because of a cold.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は風邪[かぜ]で学[がっ]校[こう]を休[やす]みました。

example_sentences.japanese: 風邪で頭が痛いです。
example_sentences.english: My head hurts because of a cold.
example_sentences.furigana: 風邪[かぜ]で頭[あたま]が痛[いた]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 母は風邪です。
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は風邪[かぜ]です。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the medicine shelf sits past the onigiri, a lonely row of blister packs nobody touches — until 2 a.m., when someone stumbles in hacking and coughing, sweeps the whole row into a basket, and pays without a word. That row of boxes is the medicine.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi restocks the shelf with only a <reading>cursory</reading> glance, tossing boxes on by feel. A customer mumbles '<reading>くすり</reading>, please' without looking up either — both of them running on autopilot at 2 a.m., neither one fully awake.

example_sentences.japanese: 朝と晩に薬を飲みます。
example_sentences.english: I take medicine in the morning and at night.
example_sentences.furigana: 朝[あさ]と晩[ばん]に薬[くすり]を飲[の]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 薬を病院でもらいました。
example_sentences.english: I got the medicine at the hospital.
example_sentences.furigana: 薬[くすり]を病[びょう]院[いん]でもらいました。

example_sentences.japanese: 薬をかばんに入れました。
example_sentences.english: I put the medicine in my bag.
example_sentences.furigana: 薬[くすり]をかばんに入[い]れました。

items.mnemonic_text: A drawing of the land: chizu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail, a hiker stalls at an unmarked fork, digs a single folded sheet out of her pack, and traces the dotted line with her finger all the way to the vending machine waiting improbably at the summit. That creased sheet in her hands is the map that gets her there.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the fork she unfolds it and mutters '<reading>cheese zoo</reading>' under her breath — her own private trick for the sound — tracing the line with one finger: '<reading>ちず</reading>, cheese zoo, don't you dare blow away now.'

example_sentences.japanese: 地図をかばんに入れました。
example_sentences.english: I put the map in my bag.
example_sentences.furigana: 地[ち]図[ず]をかばんに入[い]れました。

example_sentences.japanese: この地図は古いです。
example_sentences.furigana: この地[ち]図[ず]は古[ふる]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 地図で駅を見つけました。
example_sentences.english: I found the station on the map.
example_sentences.furigana: 地[ち]図[ず]で駅[えき]を見[み]つけました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank crossing, the ferryman won't push off until every passenger hands him a small paper stub, torn cleanly in half at the perforation. No stub, no ride across — that torn scrap clutched in your hand is the ticket.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the ferryman drops each torn stub into a rusty tin he calls his '<reading>key pool</reading>,' clinking it in with a grin and calling out '<reading>きっぷ</reading>, another one for the pile' before shoving off.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅で切符を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a ticket at the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]で切[きっ]符[ぷ]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は切符をかばんに入れました。
example_sentences.english: I put the ticket in my bag.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は切[きっ]符[ぷ]をかばんに入[い]れました。

example_sentences.japanese: その切符を友達にあげました。
example_sentences.english: I gave that ticket to my friend.
example_sentences.furigana: その切[きっ]符[ぷ]を友[とも]達[だち]にあげました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, Koichi refuses to leave any bag at the bottom, so he hauls all of them past the vending machine at the summit, knees creaking louder with every step. By the time he collapses at the top, all anyone can see is baggage — two duffels, a rolled tent, and Koichi somewhere underneath it all.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi reaches the vending machine at the trail's summit and groans, 'need... motsu... one more step,' shifting the duffel on his shoulder. A hiker behind him hears only <reading>にもつ</reading> — sounds just like <reading>need-motsu</reading> to her, watching him stagger under all that luggage.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は荷物を持って駅に行きました。
example_sentences.english: I carried my luggage to the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は荷[に]物[もつ]を持[も]って駅[えき]に行[い]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: その荷物はとても重いです。
example_sentences.furigana: その荷[に]物[もつ]はとても重[おも]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼が私の荷物を運んでくれました。
example_sentences.english: He carried my luggage for me.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]が私[わたし]の荷[に]物[もつ]を運[はこ]んでくれました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the overhead cart — that boxy frame with its axle drawn straight through, the <kanji>vehicle</kanji> shape you already know — gets struck by the same jagged bolt that cracks out of the rain-soaked sky, feeding it pure <kanji>electricity</kanji>. Sparks race down the axle and the whole cart screams off along the tracks, electrified into a train.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>でんしゃ</reading> is just 電's でん plus 車's しゃ said back to back — the readings you already know, joined.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎朝電車で学校へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to school by train every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]電[でん]車[しゃ]で学[がっ]校[こう]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅で電車を待ちました。
example_sentences.english: I waited for the train at the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]で電[でん]車[しゃ]を待[ま]ちました。

example_sentences.japanese: その電車はとても速いです。
example_sentences.furigana: その電[でん]車[しゃ]はとても速[はや]いです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Outside Koichi's konbini, under the buzzing fluorescent sign, that same overhead cart shape — axle through the middle, wheels flanking each side, the boxy frame all around — rolls up to the beeping till lane itself, engine running. Nobody laid a track out here, just four wheels parked on the apron: a <kanji>car</kanji>, plain and simple.
items.reading_mnemonic: This is the same 車 you already read as くるま, so the word for car is simply <reading>くるま</reading> — the reading you learned with the kanji itself.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は新しい車を買いました。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は新[あたら]しい車[くるま]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼の車は駅の近くにあります。
example_sentences.english: His car is near the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]の車[くるま]は駅[えき]の近[ちか]くにあります。

example_sentences.japanese: 車の中に犬がいます。
example_sentences.english: There is a dog inside the car.
example_sentences.furigana: 車[くるま]の中[なか]に犬[いぬ]がいます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the overhead cart shape — axle through the center, wheels braced on either side, the same boxy frame you already know as a <kanji>vehicle</kanji> — comes loose from its cart body and rolls itself up the mossy steps on just its two wheels, wobbling past the enormous bell while cats scatter. No engine, no rails, just those wheels pedaling themselves uphill: a bicycle.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cat at Grandma Kane's shrine watches the wheels totter past the bell and yowls, 'jitters... shaa!' as they nearly tip into the moss. That startled <reading>jitters-sha</reading> cry is exactly how you say bicycle: <reading>じてんしゃ</reading>.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎日自転車で学校に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to school by bicycle every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]日[にち]自[じ]転[てん]車[しゃ]で学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 弟は新しい自転車が欲しいです。
example_sentences.english: My younger brother wants a new bicycle.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]は新[あたら]しい自[じ]転[てん]車[しゃ]が欲[ほ]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 公園に自転車がたくさんあります。
example_sentences.english: There are a lot of bicycles at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]に自[じ]転[てん]車[しゃ]がたくさんあります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The restless figure who can't stand still — always mid-stride, always about to <kanji>go</kanji> somewhere — sprints down a runway and just keeps going, faster and faster, until the ground drops away entirely and he's roaring into the sky strapped inside an airplane.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, gets impatient waiting for delivery trucks, so he buys a tiny plane. Swooping over the store, he yells his restock call — <reading>"HEE, GO KEY!"</reading> — and that shout becomes <reading>ひこうき</reading>, the sound of his little airplane roaring past overhead.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は飛行機で日本へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I'm going to Japan by airplane.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は飛[ひ]行[こう]機[き]で日本[にほん]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: あの飛行機は空を大変低く飛んでいます。
example_sentences.english: That airplane over there is flying very low across the sky.
example_sentences.furigana: あの飛[ひ]行[こう]機[き]は空[そら]を大[たい]変[へん]低[ひく]く飛[と]んでいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 空港で飛行機を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I saw an airplane at the airport.
example_sentences.furigana: 空[くう]港[こう]で飛[ひ]行[こう]機[き]を見[み]ました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: An otter drags every barrel and plank he can find onto the riverbank, lashing them together into a lopsided raft before the current rises further. He shoves off with a broom for a paddle — proof that any floating hunk of junk counts as a ship the moment it carries someone somewhere.
items.reading_mnemonic: The ferryman blows through a battered <reading>funnel</reading> to signal departure, and the honk that comes out lands squarely as <reading>ふね</reading> — the noise every boat on this river makes before it pushes off from the dock.

example_sentences.japanese: 船で海を渡ります。
example_sentences.english: We cross the sea by ship.
example_sentences.furigana: 船[ふね]で海[うみ]を渡[わた]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は今船に乗っています。
example_sentences.english: He's on the ship right now.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は今[いま]船[ふね]に乗[の]っています。

example_sentences.japanese: あの船は大きいです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, the sun crawls across the sky the way it does at the shrine, ticking off <kanji>hours</kanji> like a clock reflected in the water. Between one splash of laundry and the next, the gate-shaped gap of caught sunlight marks the <kanji>interval</kanji> you were gone, and you realize you've lost several whole hours just watching the current.
items.reading_mnemonic: Regular reading — 時（じ）plus 間（かん）simply combine, giving you <reading>じかん</reading> straight from readings you already know.

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日、勉強の時間があります。
example_sentences.english: I have time to study every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]、勉[べん]強[きょう]の時[じ]間[かん]があります。

example_sentences.japanese: 授業の時間は九十分です。
example_sentences.furigana: 授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]の時[じ]間[かん]は九[きゅう]十[じゅう]分[ふん]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 待つ時間が長いです。
example_sentences.furigana: 待[ま]つ時[じ]間[かん]が長[なが]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: The hour on the clock: ji.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till clock is nothing but that same sun-in-a-window face from the shrine, glowing under fluorescent lights instead of sky. The beeping till freezes the instant the hand lands square on a number, and Koichi calls out that exact moment — not a stretch of <kanji>time</kanji>, just the single instant the sun-face points to.
items.reading_mnemonic: Regular reading — 時 was already taught as <reading>じ</reading>, and that's exactly the reading this word keeps, unchanged.

example_sentences.japanese: 今何時ですか。
example_sentences.furigana: 今[いま]何[なん]時[じ]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 授業は九時に始まります。
example_sentences.furigana: 授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]は九[きゅう]時[じ]に始[はじ]まります。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は七時に起きました。
example_sentences.english: I woke up at seven o'clock.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は七[なな]時[じ]に起[お]きました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The woodcutter owns no clock. One clean swing through a log takes him exactly one <kanji>minute</kanji>, so when the villagers ask how long the noodles need, he answers in logs and starts chopping. Twelve leaning <kanji>parts</kanji> later the noodles are done: count the halves, halve the count, and you have counted minutes.
items.reading_mnemonic: This is just 分 wearing its taught reading, so a number plus <reading>ふん</reading> counts your minutes.
items.description: Attaches to a number to count minutes and to give clock times. The sound shifts after several numbers — one, three, four, six, eight and ten — so those number-plus-minutes combinations are worth learning as fixed forms rather than assembling them.

example_sentences.japanese: 会議は三十分ぐらいでした。
example_sentences.english: The meeting was about thirty minutes long.
example_sentences.furigana: 会[かい]議[ぎ]は三[さん]十[じゅう]分[ふん]ぐらいでした。

example_sentences.japanese: 五分待ってください。
example_sentences.furigana: 五[ご]分[ふん]待[ま]ってください。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅まで五分歩きました。
example_sentences.english: I walked five minutes to the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]まで五[ご]分[ふん]歩[ある]きました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Partway up the mountain trail, a hiker's runaway balloon slips its string and drifts higher than the vending machine at the summit, then higher than the whole ridge — it doesn't stop until it's the very mark of <kanji>up</kanji> itself, floating above everything below it: to go up, rise.
items.reading_mnemonic: On that same trail, a hiker named Agatha grabs the balloon's string by mistake and is yanked skyward, yelling 「<reading>あがる</reading>」 as she rises past the summit — the sound of her cry, <reading>ah-ga-roo</reading>, is exactly how you say to go up, rise.

example_sentences.japanese: 毎朝、二階に上がって窓を開けます。
example_sentences.english: Every morning I go up to the second floor and open the window.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]朝[あさ]、二[に]階[かい]に上[あ]がって窓[まど]を開[あ]けます。

example_sentences.japanese: 雨が上がったら、公園を歩きましょう。
example_sentences.english: Once the rain stops, let's walk in the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 雨[あめ]が上[あ]がったら、公[こう]園[えん]を歩[ある]きましょう。

example_sentences.japanese: 家に上がる前に靴を脱ぎます。
example_sentences.english: I take off my shoes before entering the house.
example_sentences.furigana: 家[いえ]に上[あ]がる前[まえ]に靴[くつ]を脱[ぬ]ぎます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat swats the offering shelf until the charm hanging beneath it swings loose, dropping further and further past the mossy steps — everything about it points one way, straight <kanji>below</kanji> where it used to sit: to go down, fall.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow perches on the shrine's bell rope, but her weight drags it lower and lower until it dips past the mossy steps — she squawks a mournful 「<reading>さがる</reading>」, her cry sounding just like <reading>saga-ru</reading>, as she watches herself sink: to go down, fall.

example_sentences.japanese: 飛行機が下がりました。
example_sentences.furigana: 飛[ひ]行[こう]機[き]が下[さ]がりました。

example_sentences.japanese: 声が少し下がりました。
example_sentences.furigana: 声[こえ]が少[すこ]し下[さ]がりました。

example_sentences.japanese: パンが百円に下がりました。
example_sentences.english: The bread's price dropped to 100 yen.
example_sentences.furigana: パンが百[ひゃく]円[えん]に下[さ]がりました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a kid raises his hand so high above his desk it nearly brushes the ceiling, then keeps going — hoisting his chair, his bag, even the wastebasket until everything in the room sits <kanji>above</kanji> where it started: to raise.
items.reading_mnemonic: In the echoing hallway, the same kid hoists the trophy case higher, grunting 「<reading>あげる</reading>」 with each heave, the sound landing right on <reading>ah-geh-roo</reading> — pure effort to raise something up.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は手を上げました。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は手[て]を上[あ]げました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は顔を上げました。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は顔[かお]を上[あ]げました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は声を上げました。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は声[こえ]を上[あ]げました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The shelf from 下 tilts, and the crate riding on it slides toward that dangling mark, sliding <kanji>down, below</kanji> the shelf's edge until it's about to hit the floor on its own. Before that happens you grab the crate and lower it yourself, hand over hand, taking it down deliberately instead of letting gravity finish the job.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow perches above Koichi's konbini loading dock, puffing little flames as a signal. The clerks call back "<reading>oh, rose</reading>!" mishearing his screech for a flower, but they still know to <reading>おろす</reading> the delivery crates, lowering box after box off the truck onto the pavement.

example_sentences.japanese: 机の上から本を下ろしました。
example_sentences.english: I took the book down from on top of the desk.
example_sentences.furigana: 机[つくえ]の上[うえ]から本[ほん]を下[お]ろしました。

example_sentences.japanese: かばんを椅子の下に下ろしてください。
example_sentences.english: Please put your bag down under the chair.
example_sentences.furigana: かばんを椅[い]子[す]の下[した]に下[お]ろしてください。

example_sentences.japanese: 父は荷物を車から下ろしました。

example_sentences.furigana: 父[ちち]は荷[に]物[もつ]を車[くるま]から下[お]ろしました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker's phone slips loose from an unzipped pocket and tumbles by itself past the vending machine, bouncing down switchback after switchback with nobody chasing it. Nobody pushed it, nobody dropped it on purpose — it just goes, all the way down into the ravine below, entirely on its own.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a tanuki named Otchi loses his footing on the loose gravel and yelps "<reading>ouchy</reading>!" as he tumbles past the vending machine. His cry is how you remember <reading>おちる</reading>, the verb for anything that simply falls on its own.

example_sentences.japanese: 机から鉛筆が落ちました。
example_sentences.english: The pencil fell off the desk.
example_sentences.furigana: 机[つくえ]から鉛[えん]筆[ぴつ]が落[お]ちました。

example_sentences.japanese: 秋に木から葉が落ちます。
example_sentences.english: In autumn, leaves fall from the trees.
example_sentences.furigana: 秋[あき]に木[き]から葉[は]が落[お]ちます。

example_sentences.japanese: 財布がかばんから落ちましたよ。
example_sentences.english: Your wallet fell out of your bag.
example_sentences.furigana: 財[さい]布[ふ]がかばんから落[お]ちましたよ。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a boy juggling erasers by the sports field takes aim and flings one straight down onto his rival's shoe, on purpose, then strolls off whistling. Nobody trips him, nothing slips — he means to send it down, and that deliberate act of sending something down is the whole word.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a boy named Otto stands at the sports field fence and shouts "<reading>oh, toss</reading> it here!" before yanking the ball straight down out of the air himself. That shout is how you remember <reading>おとす</reading>, the verb for deliberately dropping something.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は財布を落としました。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は財[さい]布[ふ]を落[お]としました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女はかばんを駅で落としました。
example_sentences.english: She dropped her bag at the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]はかばんを駅[えき]で落[お]としました。

example_sentences.japanese: 弟は傘を公園で落としました。
example_sentences.english: My younger brother dropped his umbrella at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 弟[おとうと]は傘[かさ]を公[こう]園[えん]で落[お]としました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one of the many cats steals an offering plate from beneath the enormous bell, but the mossy steps make for a terrible getaway. Guilt, or maybe just clumsiness, wins out, and by dawn the cat has quietly carried the plate all the way back to the exact spot it took it from.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat flings a fish bone past the enormous bell, and every time it sails back into her paw the bell gives one clean "<reading>kay-essu</reading>" clang. That clang is <reading>かえす</reading>, the sound of something coming right back to where it started.

example_sentences.japanese: 図書館で本を返します。
example_sentences.english: I return the book at the library.
example_sentences.furigana: 図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で本[ほん]を返[かえ]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達にペンを返しました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank the current is too fast to wade, so instead of crossing yourself you stretch out and hand the umbrella straight across to the woman waiting on the far bank. She catches it one-handed, dry the whole time — you didn't cross the river, you handed it over.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a cat drags a stray pot of stew up the mossy steps and dumps it at your feet. '<reading>What a stew</reading>,' you mutter — <reading>わたす</reading> — as Grandma Kane scolds you for feeding the shrine cats her prized dinner.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は彼に本を渡します。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は彼[かれ]に本[ほん]を渡[わた]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 母は毎朝私に弁当を渡します。
example_sentences.english: My mother hands me a boxed lunch every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]私[わたし]に弁[べん]当[とう]を渡[わた]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は駅員に切符を渡した。
example_sentences.english: She handed her ticket to the station staff.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は駅[えき]員[いん]に切[きっ]符[ぷ]を渡[わた]した。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You wake with the sun already high, sprint to Sei's school still wearing one shoe, and skid into the echoing hallway just as the bell finishes its last ring. Every other seat is filled, every face turned toward the door, toward you, standing there late.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei tears down the mountain trail toward school, trips over a root by the lone vending machine, and yells '<reading>oh, curry!</reading>' as his lunchbox bursts open — <reading>おくれる</reading> — arriving with rice down his shirt and the bell already silent.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日、学校に遅れました。
example_sentences.english: I was late for school today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、学[がっ]校[こう]に遅[おく]れました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼はいつも会議に遅れる。
example_sentences.english: He is always late for meetings.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]はいつも会[かい]議[ぎ]に遅[おく]れる。

example_sentences.furigana: バスが遅[おく]れて、駅[えき]で待[ま]ちました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The last train chimes its warning right outside Koichi's konbini, and you abandon your basket mid-scan, shove past the onigiri shelf, and pelt for the platform doors as they begin to slide shut. There's no time left to think — only to hurry.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cat bolts down the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine for no reason at all, and you chase after it shouting '<reading>easy, go, easy, go!</reading>' — <reading>いそぐ</reading> — sprinting the whole way down before the enormous bell finishes its first toll.

example_sentences.furigana: 電[でん]車[しゃ]の時[じ]間[かん]ですから、急[いそ]ぎましょう。

example_sentences.furigana: 急[いそ]がないでください。時[じ]間[かん]はたくさんあります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini till is buried under boxes he can't shift alone, so you hold up your <kanji>hand</kanji>, fingers spread the way you always picture it, and slide it under the heaviest crate just before it tips. You're not doing his job for him — you're only lending a <kanji>hand</kanji>, which is exactly what helping means.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the sports field at Sei's school, your friend can't lift the net alone, so you jog over saying '<reading>let's do</reading> this together' — <reading>てつだう</reading> — and grab the other end before he drops it.
items.description: 手伝う specifically means pitching in on a task that's mainly someone else's — helping with chores, homework, or work — rather than a general word for rescuing or assisting in any sense.

example_sentences.japanese: 母は忙しいので、私は料理を手伝いました。

example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は忙[いそが]しいので、私[わたし]は料[りょう]理[り]を手伝[てつだ]いました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You are locked out of your apartment in the rain, keys sitting in plain view on the kitchen counter through the window, phone dead, neighbor not home. You stand under the awning testing the same doorknob for the tenth time, and this exact useless loop is the meaning: to be troubled.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, a scruffy kangaroo blocks your way, its fur knotted with burrs. You crouch down and <reading>comb a roo</reading> right there on the gravel, and the line of hikers behind you groans, thoroughly <reading>こまる</reading> at the wait.

example_sentences.english: I'm troubled because I don't have any money.
example_sentences.furigana: お金[かね]がなくて困[こま]っています。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は問題が難しくて困った。
example_sentences.english: He was troubled because the problem was difficult.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は問[もん]題[だい]が難[むずか]しくて困[こま]った。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The supply cabinet at your office has exactly one stapler, and by Friday afternoon it is simply gone — not broken, not borrowed, gone. You check the same empty shelf three times as if it might reappear. That total vanishing, the running-out-to-nothing, is the meaning: to disappear, to run out.
items.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a woodpecker hammers the same dead branch for hours until it finally splits and topples into the current. The birds go quiet — <reading>knock, no more</reading> — and the fisherman sighs: whatever was there has become <reading>なくなる</reading>, gone for good.

example_sentences.japanese: 財布の中のお金が無くなりました。
example_sentences.english: The money in my wallet ran out.
example_sentences.furigana: 財[さい]布[ふ]の中[なか]のお金[かね]が無[な]くなりました。

example_sentences.english: The eggs at home ran out.
example_sentences.furigana: 家[いえ]の卵[たまご]が無[な]くなりました。

example_sentences.japanese: 机の上の鉛筆が無くなりました。
example_sentences.english: The pencil on the desk disappeared.
example_sentences.furigana: 机[つくえ]の上[うえ]の鉛[えん]筆[ぴつ]が無[な]くなりました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: After the birthday party ends and the last guest waves goodbye, one lonely slice of cake sits alone on the table, uneaten, crumbs scattered everywhere else. Everyone else got their piece and left; only this slice stayed behind. That staying-behind, the leftover, is the meaning: to remain.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the last onigiri on the shelf turns out to be a display fake with <reading>no core</reading> — just rice on the outside, hollow within. Koichi leaves it sitting there past closing, the one item that never sells: it simply <reading>のこる</reading>, remains, night after night.

example_sentences.japanese: パンが少し残った。
example_sentences.english: A little bread was left over.
example_sentences.furigana: パンが少[すこ]し残[のこ]った。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は部屋に残った。
example_sentences.english: He stayed behind in the room.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は部屋[へや]に残[のこ]った。

example_sentences.japanese: 時間が少し残っています。
example_sentences.furigana: 時[じ]間[かん]が少[すこ]し残[のこ]っています。

items.meaning_mnemonic: You watch an intersection from the corner for a full minute: the light is red, then amber, then green, then back to red, cars stopping and starting each time. Nothing about the pole itself moves, yet everything it signals is different every time you look. That shifting-in-place is the meaning: to change.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school sports field, someone drives a tiny toy car through a puddle shaped exactly like a <reading>car wash</reading>, and it rolls out a completely different color than it went in. Sei blinks at the repainted car and mutters that everything on this field has just <reading>かわる</reading>, changed.

example_sentences.japanese: 天気がよく変わります。
example_sentences.furigana: 天[てん]気[き]がよく変[か]わります。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は変わりました。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は変[か]わりました。

example_sentences.japanese: この町は変わりましたね。
example_sentences.english: This town has changed, hasn't it?
example_sentences.furigana: この町[まち]は変[か]わりましたね。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a courier frog named Kaera swaps one basket for another on every crossing — rice one way, laundry the other, never both at once. She doesn't just move things, she changes what's in someone else's hands entirely. That deliberate swap is what the word teaches: something changes because someone changed it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaera the frog announces each swap with a croak that sounds like <reading>かえる</reading> — the vendors nearby just call her <reading>Kaera</reading>, and the name stuck to the sound itself.
items.description: This is the transitive verb — you change something (someone changes their mind, changes the schedule), always with an object. There's a separate intransitive partner meaning something changes on its own; that one takes a different reading, so don't reach for this word when nothing did the changing.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は仕事を変えます。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は仕[し]事[ごと]を変[か]えます。

example_sentences.japanese: 部屋の色を変えました。
example_sentences.english: I changed the color of the room.
example_sentences.furigana: 部屋[へや]の色[いろ]を変[か]えました。

example_sentences.japanese: 名前を変えてもいいですか。
example_sentences.english: Is it okay to change my name?
example_sentences.furigana: 名[な]前[まえ]を変[か]えてもいいですか。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one of the countless cats leaps for a moth and misses, slamming into the enormous mossy bell instead. The whole hillside goes still for a second, then the bell answers — one huge sound rolling down the steps. Nobody rang it on purpose; it simply rang, sound arriving as a consequence, not a choice.
items.reading_mnemonic: The shrine cat is named <reading>Naru</reading>, and when she yowls at the bell it answers with a tone the locals swear sounds just like her name — <reading>なる</reading> — echoing down the steps every time.

example_sentences.japanese: 電話が鳴りました。
example_sentences.furigana: 電[でん]話[わ]が鳴[な]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 時計が鳴ると、起きます。
example_sentences.english: When the clock rings, I get up.
example_sentences.furigana: 時計[とけい]が鳴[な]ると、起[お]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 携帯が鳴っています。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Near the top of the steep mountain trail, the one lonely vending machine keeps its light on all night, a single bright square glowing over the dark ridge. Hikers exhausted from the climb spot it from three switchbacks away before anything else on the mountain — the machine's whole purpose, up here, is simply to shine.

items.reading_mnemonic: Customers call that drifting stuff the mascot's <reading>fur</reading>, and the clerk mutters the word every time it happens — <reading>ふる</reading> — since in this konbini it never rains, it just falls.
items.description: This verb is reserved for rain and snow falling from the sky — it doesn't extend to objects falling in general, so don't reach for it when something merely drops or tips over.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You leave the house and immediately start replaying the stove, the door, the iron — did you actually turn them off? That spiral of manufactured dread, dragging you back home just to check, is what it feels like to worry.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail, the vending machine at the summit isn't real — it never has cold drinks, it's always one more switchback past your last break, and it vanishes the moment you actually reach the top. Everyone who's hiked that trail knows the machine at the peak is only ever a dream.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the base of the mountain trail, a sign reads '<reading>you may</reading> rest here, traveler' — but climb further and the exact same sign keeps reappearing, word for word, at every switchback. That dug-up, countable stack is cash.

It isn't broken, it's just deciding what altitude is worth. That flickering number, haggling with your exhaustion, is the price you paid to get here.

items.meaning_mnemonic: That same spear, driven clean through the mouth-shaped opening, doesn't stop at one skewer — it pins three coins to the shrine step in a perfect row, and no matter how Grandma Kane's cats bat at the ends, the spear always balances dead level at its <kanji>middle, inside</kanji> point. Whatever sits there, exactly equidistant from both edges, is the center — the true middle.
items.reading_mnemonic: Chuu marches to the exact middle of the shrine steps and refuses to budge, topknot bobbing, no matter how the cats circle him. When Grandma Kane asks where he's planted himself, he squeaks the answer proudly: <reading>まんなか</reading> — <reading>the man in the middle</reading> — dead center, not one step off.

example_sentences.japanese: 公園の真ん中に犬がいます。
example_sentences.english: There's a dog in the middle of the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]の真[ま]ん中[なか]に犬[いぬ]がいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 部屋の真ん中にテーブルを置きました。
example_sentences.english: I put the table in the middle of the room.
example_sentences.furigana: 部屋[へや]の真[ま]ん中[なか]にテーブルを置[お]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 町の真ん中に大きい木があります。
example_sentences.english: There's a big tree in the middle of the town.
example_sentences.furigana: 町[まち]の真[ま]ん中[なか]に大[おお]きい木[き]があります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail swaps its steep dirt slope for a perfectly cut staircase overnight, one vending machine still stranded at the very top like nothing changed. Climbers now count each step aloud, relieved someone finally built proper stairs instead of a slope.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Sei's school, a boy named Kai races his friend Dan up the new staircase, shouting a countdown as they climb: <reading>かいだん</reading> — <reading>Kai, Dan</reading> — one name per step, over and over, until they reach the landing out of breath. Stairs, and the boys who race them.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は階段を上がりました。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は階[かい]段[だん]を上[あ]がりました。

example_sentences.japanese: 階段の下に猫がいました。
example_sentences.english: There was a cat at the bottom of the stairs.
example_sentences.furigana: 階[かい]段[だん]の下[した]に猫[ねこ]がいました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は階段を降りて外に出た。
example_sentences.english: She went down the stairs and went outside.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は階[かい]段[だん]を降[お]りて外[そと]に出[で]た。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A vending machine sits at the very top of the mountain trail, impossible to reach on foot. Some hiker gave up climbing years ago and bolted a box to the cliff face that just goes straight up, dinging at each impossible landing until the doors slide open right onto the summit. That box is the elevator.
items.reading_mnemonic: エレベーター is a katakana loanword straight from English, so saying <reading>elevator</reading> is saying <reading>エレベーター</reading> — the sound is the whole word, no decoding needed.

example_sentences.japanese: エレベーターは五階で止まりました。
example_sentences.english: The elevator stopped on the fifth floor.
example_sentences.furigana: エレベーターは五[ご]階[かい]で止[と]まりました。

example_sentences.japanese: 私はエレベーターに乗ります。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はエレベーターに乗[の]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: エレベーターの中に猫がいました。
example_sentences.english: There was a cat inside the elevator.
example_sentences.furigana: エレベーターの中[なか]に猫[ねこ]がいました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's mossy shrine steps got tired of climbers stopping to catch their breath, so one day the whole staircase started crawling upward on its own, each step sliding onto the next in an endless diagonal parade. The shrine cats ride it like a conveyor belt straight past the enormous bell. That self-walking staircase is the escalator.
items.reading_mnemonic: エスカレーター is a katakana loanword straight from English, so saying <reading>escalator</reading> is saying <reading>エスカレーター</reading> — the sound is the whole word.

example_sentences.japanese: エスカレーターはどこですか。
example_sentences.furigana: エスカレーターはどこですか。

example_sentences.japanese: デパートにエスカレーターがあります。
example_sentences.english: There's an escalator in the department store.
example_sentences.furigana: デパートにエスカレーターがあります。

example_sentences.japanese: 私はエレベーターよりエスカレーターが好きです。
example_sentences.english: I like escalators more than elevators.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はエレベーターよりエスカレーターが好[す]きです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini has one doorway low enough that you have to duck your head to step through — that's the ducking figure who <kanji>enters</kanji>. Beyond it the sliding doors gape like a giant <kanji>mouth</kanji>, wide open all night, swallowing customers whole. Duck, then get swallowed by the mouth: that gaping doorway is the entrance.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi hangs a mock sign over the gaping doorway reading <reading>いりぐち</reading>, joking it looks like the entrance to an <reading>eerie Gucci</reading> boutique — pure velvet-rope energy for a konbini. Duck under, get swallowed by the mouth, and you've found the entrance.

example_sentences.japanese: 入口はどこですか。
example_sentences.furigana: 入[いり]口[ぐち]はどこですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 図書館の入口に猫がいました。
example_sentences.english: There was a cat at the entrance of the library.
example_sentences.furigana: 図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]の入[いり]口[ぐち]に猫[ねこ]がいました。

example_sentences.japanese: 入口で友達を待ちました。
example_sentences.english: I waited for my friend at the entrance.
example_sentences.furigana: 入[いり]口[ぐち]で友[とも]達[だち]を待[ま]ちました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Two mountains stacked one on top of the other are already more <kanji>exit</kanji> than anyone wants to climb, so the exhausted hiker at Koichi's konbini rest stop bolts for the nearest gaping <kanji>mouth</kanji> of a doorway instead of scaling a third summit. Two mountains too many plus a wide-open mouth: that's the exit.
items.reading_mnemonic: 出 read で and 口 read ぐち combine exactly as taught, giving <reading>でぐち</reading> straight from the parts you already know.

example_sentences.japanese: 出口はどこですか。
example_sentences.furigana: 出[で]口[ぐち]はどこですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 出口は左にあります。
example_sentences.english: The exit is on the left.
example_sentences.furigana: 出[で]口[ぐち]は左[ひだり]にあります。

example_sentences.japanese: 出口を探しています。
example_sentences.furigana: 出[で]口[ぐち]を探[さが]しています。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi cuts one narrow slot into his konbini's front glass so customers never have to walk inside - just an open <kanji>mouth</kanji> in the pane, nothing else. You slide your money through it, a voice on the other side takes your order, and that slot is the service window.
items.reading_mnemonic: A customer once tracked <reading>muddy goo</reading> straight up to Koichi's register, so he cut that slot to keep boots outside entirely. Now everyone hands their cash through the gap instead of walking in, and he calls the whole setup the <reading>まどぐち</reading> - the window that keeps the mud out.

example_sentences.japanese: 銀行の窓口はどこですか。
example_sentences.furigana: 銀[ぎん]行[こう]の窓[まど]口[ぐち]はどこですか。

example_sentences.japanese: その窓口で切符を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought the ticket at that window.
example_sentences.furigana: その窓[まど]口[ぐち]で切[きっ]符[ぷ]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 窓口の人は親切です。
example_sentences.english: The person at the window is kind.
example_sentences.furigana: 窓[まど]口[ぐち]の人[ひと]は親[しん]切[せつ]です。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Your dresser has a wooden box wedged into it like a second peak stacked on the mountain of drawers above it. Tug the handle and the box finally does what its shape always threatened: it does its best <kanji>exit / leave</kanji> impression, sliding all the way out and dumping your socks on the floor. That sliding box is the drawer.
items.reading_mnemonic: Hana sprints across the library the moment a card-catalog drawer jams, calling it her <reading>hickey dash</reading> - the mad scramble to yank it loose before it swallows someone's fingers. Everyone now calls the stuck drawer itself the <reading>ひきだし</reading>, since it's always the reason for her sprint.

example_sentences.japanese: 机の引き出しに鍵があります。
example_sentences.english: There's a key in the desk drawer.
example_sentences.furigana: 机[つくえ]の引[ひ]き出[だ]しに鍵[かぎ]があります。

example_sentences.japanese: 引き出しの中にお金があります。
example_sentences.furigana: 引[ひ]き出[だ]しの中[なか]にお金[かね]があります。

example_sentences.japanese: 引き出しを開けて写真を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I opened the drawer and looked at the photos.
example_sentences.furigana: 引[ひ]き出[だ]しを開[あ]けて写[しゃ]真[しん]を見[み]ました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Every night at Grandma Kane's shrine, the rice offerings spoil in the heat before the cats even get to them, so the priest wedges a tall humming metal locker in beside the mossy steps. It breathes cold air and keeps everything frost-stiff till morning. Villagers just call the humming locker the refrigerator.
items.reading_mnemonic: Rei keeps a penguin egg in Koichi's walk-in cooler and insists on calling the whole humming steel box her <reading>ray's zoo crate</reading>, since it's the only place cold enough for it. The other clerks shortened that to <reading>れいぞうこ</reading>, and now it just means the fridge.

example_sentences.japanese: 冷蔵庫に卵と牛乳があります。
example_sentences.english: There are eggs and milk in the refrigerator.
example_sentences.furigana: 冷[れい]蔵[ぞう]庫[こ]に卵[たまご]と牛[ぎゅう]乳[にゅう]があります。

example_sentences.japanese: 肉を冷蔵庫に入れました。
example_sentences.english: I put the meat in the refrigerator.
example_sentences.furigana: 肉[にく]を冷[れい]蔵[ぞう]庫[こ]に入[い]れました。

example_sentences.furigana: 冷[れい]蔵[ぞう]庫[こ]の中[なか]に飲[の]み物[もの]がありますか。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Everyone at the riverbank campsite balances their food on flat stones fished out of the water, one apiece, since nobody packed real ones. It works fine until the stones tip over the second a fish bone hits them. What the trip actually needed was a proper plate.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sara refuses to eat off river stones like the rest of the campers and packs an actual dish for every single meal. The others tease that of course <reading>Sara</reading> brought her own <reading>さら</reading> - it's practically her name.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は皿を洗いました。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は皿[さら]を洗[あら]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 皿の上に肉があります。
example_sentences.furigana: 皿[さら]の上[うえ]に肉[にく]があります。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女はテーブルに皿を置いた。

example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]はテーブルに皿[さら]を置[お]いた。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the cats never come for the incense — they come for what's set beside it: a chipped ceramic bowl brimming with warm rice, left out every evening as an offering. By the time the bell stops ringing, every cat in the yard is circling that single rice bowl.
items.reading_mnemonic: The head priest only allows one bowl of rice per cat, so he stands by the bell shouting <reading>ちゃわん</reading> — which lands in your ear as <reading>Cha, one!</reading> — one cry per cat, one bowl each, no seconds no matter how loudly they beg.

example_sentences.japanese: これは茶碗です。
example_sentences.furigana: これは茶[ちゃ]碗[わん]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 茶碗にご飯を入れました。
example_sentences.english: I put rice in the rice bowl.
example_sentences.furigana: 茶[ちゃ]碗[わん]にご飯[はん]を入[い]れました。

example_sentences.japanese: テーブルの上に茶碗があります。
example_sentences.english: There is a rice bowl on the table.
example_sentences.furigana: テーブルの上[うえ]に茶[ちゃ]碗[わん]があります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the only vending machine sits with two thin metal prongs sticking out where the coin slot should be — the last hiker jammed his chopsticks in there trying to pry loose a stuck can. Nobody's fixed it since; they just call it the chopsticks machine.
items.reading_mnemonic: By the time a hiker drags themselves up to that machine, all they can manage is a rasping <reading>はし</reading> — it comes out as <reading>ha-shh</reading>, half word, half exhale — right as they spot the two chopsticks still propping the jammed coin door open.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は箸で肉を食べます。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は箸[はし]で肉[にく]を食[た]べます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は箸を使いました。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は箸[はし]を使[つか]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: この箸は新しいです。
example_sentences.furigana: この箸[はし]は新[あたら]しいです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the hot-drink machine drops every order with a hollow knock — kop — straight into a plastic cup waiting below. Regulars just call the whole machine 'the koppu machine,' since that's the sound the cup makes catching the drink every single time.
items.reading_mnemonic: コップ is written exactly as it sounds — <reading>コップ</reading> — a katakana borrowing of the English word <reading>cup</reading>, no decoding needed.

example_sentences.japanese: そのコップは新しいです。
example_sentences.furigana: そのコップは新[あたら]しいです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: In the cafeteria at Sei's school, someone catapults a lump of mashed potato clean across the room with a spoon during lunch, and it lands with a wet slap on the sports-field banner outside the window. Every year the students blame a new first-year, and every year it's the same bent spoon.
items.reading_mnemonic: スプーン is written exactly as it sounds — <reading>スプーン</reading> — a katakana borrowing of the English word <reading>spoon</reading>, no decoding needed.

example_sentences.japanese: そのスプーンを使ってください。
example_sentences.furigana: そのスプーンを使[つか]ってください。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the till clerk jabs a four-pronged skewer into the rotating hot dog case just to see what happens, and the sausage spins loose, flies across the aisle, and lands spiked upright on the onigiri shelf like a tiny flag. Four sharp points, one impaled sausage: that whole ridiculous skewer is a fork.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>フォーク</reading> is written exactly as it sounds - a borrowed word, so it is simply the English fork clipped down into kana, nothing to decode.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a hiker too hungry to wait rams a thin blade sideways into the vending machine's coin slot, prying the stuck snack loose in one clean, mean slice before it even finishes falling. The narrow single-edged tool built for exactly that kind of job is a knife.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>ナイフ</reading> is written exactly as it sounds - it comes straight from English knife, rounded off into kana, nothing more to it.

example_sentences.japanese: 台所にナイフがあります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, someone finishing the dishes flings a soaked cloth overhead to dry it in the wind, and it sails wide, landing draped square across a passing fisherman's shoulders, soaking through his shirt before he's even noticed. That oversized wet cloth everyone keeps grabbing for and missing is a towel.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>タオル</reading> is written exactly as it sounds - a loanword from the English towel, squeezed into kana, nothing to decode.

example_sentences.japanese: 私はタオルを使いました。
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はタオルを使[つか]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 母はタオルを二枚買いました。
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]はタオルを二[に]枚[まい]買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: かばんの中にタオルがあります。
example_sentences.english: There is a towel in the bag.
example_sentences.furigana: かばんの中[なか]にタオルがあります。

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one of the resident cats bats a pale, chalky slab off the mossy steps and it tumbles straight into the offering basin, foaming white as it rolls under the water until the cat backs away, thoroughly appalled at what it started. A stone that lathers the moment it touches water is soap.
items.reading_mnemonic: A stagehand named Ken keeps a foaming stone can set backstage at the shrine's bell tower, and every time he sets the can down near water it hisses into suds; the caretaker started calling it his <reading>せっけん</reading>, the <reading>set-Ken</reading> can, and the name outlived the joke and stuck to every bar of soap since.
